chapters.n: Chronicles opens by reaching all the way back to Adam. Written after the exile, it reminds a small, discouraged community that their story belongs to God’s plan for the whole human family.

f.g: Seth, Adam’s son born after Abel’s death.

chapters.n: The list continues through the early patriarchs. Latter-day scripture adds that these men held the priesthood and were ordained by Adam.

f.g: Jared, father of Enoch.

chapters.n: Henoch is Enoch, the prophet who “walked with God.” Latter-day Saints learn much more about him and his righteous city of Zion in the book of Moses.

f.g: Enoch.

chapters.n: Noah and his three sons close the line from Adam. From these three, the next verses trace the nations of the known world after the Flood.
Japheth’s descendants are linked with peoples to the north and west of Israel, such as the Medes (Madai) and Greeks (Javan). This section follows the “Table of Nations” in Genesis 10.

f.g: Linked with the Ionians, or Greeks.

chapters.n: Gomer’s sons are associated with peoples of Asia Minor and the regions around the Black Sea.

f.g: Often linked with a region of eastern Anatolia (modern Turkey/Armenia).

chapters.n: Javan’s sons point to Mediterranean island and coastal peoples, including Cyprus (Kittim).

f.g: Cyprus, and later Mediterranean seafarers in general.
A distant seaport, possibly in Spain—the place Jonah tried to flee to.

chapters.n: Ham’s sons are tied to lands south and southwest of Israel: Cush (Ethiopia/Nubia), Mizraim (Egypt), Put (likely Libya), and Canaan.

f.g: The Hebrew name for Egypt.

chapters.n: Cush’s descendants are linked to peoples of Arabia and northeast Africa, including Sheba, famous for its queen who visited Solomon.
Nimrod is singled out as the first great warrior-ruler after the Flood, linked in Genesis with Babel and early Mesopotamian kingdoms.

f.g: Fathered; became the ancestor of.

chapters.n: Egypt’s descendants are listed as peoples (notice the plural “-im” endings), showing that these lists describe nations as well as individuals.

f.g: The “-im” ending is a Hebrew plural, marking a people group.

chapters.n: The Philistines—Israel’s great rivals in the days of Saul and David—are traced to this branch, connected with Caphtor (probably Crete).

f.g: People of Caphtor, usually identified with Crete.

chapters.n: Canaan’s line includes Sidon, the great Phoenician city, and Heth, ancestor of the Hittites.

f.g: Sidon, a major port city on the Phoenician coast.

chapters.n: These are peoples of Canaan whom Israel later encountered when it entered the promised land. The Jebusites held Jerusalem until David captured it.
More Canaanite peoples, some tied to cities along the Phoenician coast north of Israel.
The list ends with peoples of coastal and inland Syria, including Hamath, a city on Israel’s far northern frontier.

f.g: From Hamath, a city on the Orontes River in Syria.

chapters.n: Shem’s line leads toward Israel. His sons include Elam (in Persia), Asshur (Assyria) and Aram (the Arameans of Syria). The word “Semite” comes from Shem’s name.

f.g: Assyria.

chapters.n: The chosen line narrows to Arphaxad, Shelah and Eber. “Eber” may be connected with the name “Hebrew.”
Peleg’s name means “division,” recalling that in his days the earth was divided. Interpreters differ on whether this refers to Babel’s scattering of peoples or a physical division of land.
Joktan’s descendants are tied to tribes of southern Arabia.

f.g: Probably Hadhramaut, a region in southern Arabia (modern Yemen).

chapters.n: More Arabian clans descended from Joktan.

f.g: Possibly an old name for Sanaa in Yemen.

chapters.n: The list of Joktan’s sons continues; many of these names are known only here and in Genesis 10.

f.g: A second Sheba, here through Shem’s line; the name may refer to a region with several associated peoples.

chapters.n: Ophir became famous as a source of fine gold brought to Solomon.
Now the chronicler restates the line from Shem straight to Abraham, skipping the side branches. The focus is narrowing to the covenant family.
The direct line continues through Eber and Peleg.
Terah, Abraham’s father, lived in Ur of the Chaldees and, according to the book of Abraham, turned to idolatry.
The genealogy reaches Abram, whose name God changed to Abraham, “father of a multitude.” All of God’s covenant promises flow through him.
Abraham’s two eldest sons are named, with Isaac, the son of promise, listed first even though Ishmael was older.
Ishmael’s twelve sons begin with Nebaioth and Kedar, who became Arabian tribes. God had promised Ishmael would become a great nation too.

f.g: Family lines; descendants.

chapters.n: More of Ishmael’s sons, whose names match places in the Arabian desert such as Dumah and Tema.

f.g: An oasis town in northwest Arabia.

chapters.n: The list of Ishmael’s twelve sons concludes, fulfilling God’s promise that Ishmael would father twelve princes.

f.w: These are the sons of Ishmael

chapters.n: Abraham had other sons by Keturah, a secondary wife. Midian, ancestor of the Midianites, is among them—Moses’ father-in-law Jethro would be a Midianite priest.

f.g: A secondary wife with lower legal standing than a primary wife.

chapters.n: Midian’s sons are listed. The Midianites later became nomadic traders and sometimes enemies of Israel.
The line returns to Isaac and his twin sons Esau and Israel (Jacob). The chronicler uses the name Israel, the covenant name God gave Jacob.
Esau’s sons are listed, ancestors of the Edomites, Israel’s neighbors to the southeast.
Among Esau’s grandsons is Amalek, ancestor of the Amalekites who attacked Israel in the wilderness. Teman became a famous Edomite region.

f.g: In Genesis 36:12 Timna is Eliphaz’s concubine and Amalek’s mother; here the name stands in the list.

chapters.n: Reuel’s sons, more Edomite clan chiefs.
Seir was the original Horite inhabitant of the Edomite hill country; his descendants intermarried with Esau’s family.

f.g: Both a person and the mountainous region of Edom named for him.

chapters.n: Lotan’s family is listed, along with his sister Timna, who connects the Horites to Esau’s line.

f.g: Likely the source of the name Horites, the cave-dwellers or early people of Seir.

chapters.n: The clans of Shobal and Zibeon, more Horite families of Seir.
Anah’s and Dishon’s descendants. Anah’s daughter Oholibamah (Aholibamah) became one of Esau’s wives.
The Horite clans of Ezer and Dishan close this section.

f.g: A name shared with Job’s homeland, “the land of Uz” (Job 1:1), which may lie in this region.

chapters.n: Edom had kings long before Israel did. The chronicler includes them perhaps to show God’s fairness to Esau’s family and to contrast Edom’s kings with the covenant line of David to come.

f.w: before any king reigned over the children of Israel

f.g: Not the same as Balaam son of Beor, though the names are similar.

chapters.n: Edom’s kingship passed between men of different cities rather than from father to son.

f.g: A major Edomite city, later mentioned in prophecy.

chapters.n: Husham came from Teman, an Edomite region known for its wise men.
Hadad is remembered for defeating Midian in Moabite territory, a glimpse of the wars among Israel’s neighbors.

f.w: smote Midian in the field of Moab
f.g: Defeated the Midianites in the open country of Moab.

chapters.n: Samlah of Masrekah succeeds Hadad, another king from a different city.

f.g: An Edomite town, location uncertain; the name may mean “vineyard.”

chapters.n: Shaul, from Rehoboth “by the river,” takes the throne—a different man from Israel’s King Saul, though the name is the same.

f.g: Possibly the Euphrates, or a local stream in Edom.

chapters.n: Baal-hanan, whose name means “Baal is gracious,” reigns next, showing Edom’s worship of foreign gods.

f.g: “Baal is gracious”—a name honoring the Canaanite god Baal.

chapters.n: The last listed king, Hadad, is given a capital and a wife’s name and family—unusual detail in a list like this.

f.g: Her name means “God does good.”

chapters.n: After the kings come the chiefs, or clan leaders, of Edom.

f.g: Hebrew ’alluf—chiefs or clan leaders, not European nobility.

chapters.n: More Edomite chiefs, several of whose names match places in Edom.

f.g: Possibly linked with Punon, a copper-mining site where Israel camped (Numbers 33:42).

chapters.n: The chiefs of Kenaz, Teman and Mibzar, named for regions or clans.

f.g: The Kenizzites; Caleb was later called a Kenizzite (Numbers 32:12).

chapters.n: The list of Edom’s chiefs ends. Having accounted for the other branches of Abraham’s family, the chronicler is ready to focus on Israel’s sons.

f.w: These are the dukes of Edom

chapters.n: The chronicler now lists the twelve sons of Israel (Jacob), the founders of the twelve tribes. Everything that follows is organized around these families.
The list of Jacob’s sons is completed. Joseph’s sons Ephraim and Manasseh would later each count as a tribe, which is why Israel can have more than twelve tribal names.
Judah’s family comes first because David’s royal line descends from him. The chronicler does not hide the family’s sins: Judah’s firstborn Er was so wicked the Lord took his life.

f.g: A Canaanite woman.

chapters.n: Judah also had twin sons, Pharez and Zerah, by his daughter-in-law Tamar—a troubling story in Genesis 38, yet Pharez became an ancestor of David and of Jesus.

f.g: Also spelled Perez; the name means “breach” or “breaking out.”

chapters.n: Pharez’s sons. Hezron is the key figure through whom David’s line will run.
Zerah’s family included men famous for wisdom; 1 Kings compares Solomon’s wisdom favorably to that of Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Darda.

f.w: Ethan, and Heman, and Calcol, and Dara

chapters.n: Achar—called Achan in Joshua—is remembered as the man who stole forbidden plunder at Jericho and brought disaster on Israel. His name here means “trouble.”

f.g: Plunder devoted to God that was forbidden to be taken for personal use.

chapters.n: A brief note on Ethan’s son, a reminder that even the briefest family lines were worth preserving.

f.g: A very common name meaning “the LORD has helped.”

chapters.n: Hezron’s three sons are named: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai (another form of Caleb). The chapter will follow each branch.

f.g: A form of the name Caleb (see verse 18); not the same as Caleb son of Jephunneh in Joshua’s day.

chapters.n: The royal line through Ram reaches Nahshon, the leader of Judah during the wilderness journey, whose sister married Aaron.

f.w: Nahshon, prince of the children of Judah

chapters.n: Salma is the father of Boaz, the kind landowner who married Ruth the Moabitess.
From Boaz and Ruth come Obed and then Jesse, David’s father. This is the same line that closes the book of Ruth.
Jesse’s older sons are listed in birth order. Eliab was the tall eldest son Samuel first thought the Lord had chosen.

f.g: Also called Shammah or Shimeah.

chapters.n: Jesse’s fourth and fifth sons, otherwise unknown in the Bible.

f.g: “Gift of God.”

chapters.n: David is named as the seventh son. 1 Samuel mentions eight sons of Jesse; perhaps one died young or was left out here. Either way, God chose the youngest.
David’s sister Zeruiah was mother of three famous warriors: Joab, David’s army commander, and his brothers Abishai and Asahel.
David’s sister Abigail was mother of Amasa, who later commanded Absalom’s army. Her husband was an Ishmaelite, showing a mixed family heritage.

f.g: Ishmaelite; 2 Samuel 17:25 calls him an Israelite, perhaps a copying difference.

chapters.n: The genealogy turns to the line of Caleb, Hezron’s son, and his wives.

f.g: An early ancestor of the Calebite clans of southern Judah.

chapters.n: After Azubah’s death, Caleb married Ephrath, whose name is tied to Ephrathah, the area around Bethlehem.
Hur’s grandson was Bezaleel, the Spirit-filled craftsman who built the tabernacle in the wilderness.
In his later years Hezron married a daughter of Machir, from the tribe of Manasseh, linking Judah’s clans with families east of the Jordan.

f.g: Sixty.

chapters.n: Their grandson Jair controlled twenty-three towns in Gilead, east of the Jordan.
Over time Geshur and Aram took Jair’s towns and Kenath with its villages—sixty settlements in all. These lands were associated with Machir’s descendants.

f.g: A small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee.

chapters.n: After Hezron’s death his widow bore a son, Ashur, founder of Tekoa—the town that later produced the prophet Amos.

f.g: In these lists “father of” a town often means its founder or leading clan head.

chapters.n: The chronicler now follows the clans of Jerahmeel, Hezron’s firstborn, who settled in the far south of Judah.
Jerahmeel had a second wife, Atarah, mother of Onam.

f.g: Her name means “crown.”

chapters.n: Ram’s sons (a different Ram from David’s ancestor) are listed.

f.g: Not the Ram of verse 10, who was Jerahmeel’s brother.

chapters.n: Onam’s descendants continue through Shammai and Jada.

f.g: A name later famous through a Jewish rabbi of the first century BC.

chapters.n: A wife, Abihail, is named—women appear more often in Chronicles’ genealogies than one might expect.

f.g: “My father is might”; a name used for both men and women in the Bible.

chapters.n: Seled died childless, a sad note that his line ended with him.

f.g: Having no heirs was a great sorrow in Israel, since name and inheritance were passed through children.

chapters.n: Appaim’s line runs through Ishi and Sheshan.

f.g: Verse 34 says Sheshan had only daughters, so Ahlai may have been a daughter or a descendant through one.

chapters.n: Jada’s branch is recorded; another son, Jether, also died childless.

f.g: A common name; not the Jether of verse 17.

chapters.n: The direct descendants of Jerahmeel through Onam are complete.

f.w: These were the sons of Jerahmeel
f.g: A closing formula marking the end of this section.

chapters.n: Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, and an Egyptian servant named Jarha. The family line will continue in an unexpected way.

f.g: An Egyptian servant; foreigners could be adopted into Israelite families.

chapters.n: Sheshan married his daughter to Jarha, keeping the family and property alive through her. A foreign servant becomes part of Judah’s line.

f.w: gave his daughter to Jarha his servant to wife

chapters.n: The line from Jarha and Sheshan’s daughter continues through Attai and Nathan.

f.g: A different man from Nathan the prophet or Nathan son of David.

chapters.n: The generations continue, with the familiar name Obed reappearing.

f.g: Not Ruth’s son; the name (“servant”) was common.

chapters.n: More generations—this is one of the longest single lines in the chapter, carefully kept across many lifetimes.

f.g: Not the northern king Jehu; a common name meaning “the LORD is he.”

chapters.n: The line continues through Helez and Eleasah.

f.g: A name also borne by one of David’s mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:27).

chapters.n: The descendants continue through Sisamai and Shallum.

f.g: A very common name meaning “recompense” or “peace.”

chapters.n: The long line ends with Elishama, perhaps a well-known figure in the chronicler’s day. About thirteen generations from Jarha are recorded.

f.g: “God has heard.”

chapters.n: The chapter returns to Caleb’s line, focusing on towns in the Judean hills like Ziph and Hebron that his clans founded or controlled.

f.g: Here a person, but also the important city where David was first crowned.

chapters.n: Hebron’s descendants include Tappuah, also the name of a town in Judah.

f.g: “Apple”; also a town in Judah (Joshua 15:34).

chapters.n: The clans branch further, linked with towns like Jorkoam.

f.g: Probably a town in southern Judah.

chapters.n: Maon and Beth-zur, also towns in the Judean hills, are tied to this family. Maon was the home of Nabal and Abigail.
Caleb’s secondary wife Ephah bore him more sons.

f.g: A secondary wife.

chapters.n: The sons of Jahdai, whose connection to Caleb is not explained.

f.g: Perhaps another of Caleb’s wives or a descendant; the text does not say.

chapters.n: Another of Caleb’s secondary wives, Maachah, is named with her sons.

f.g: A name borne by several women in the Bible, including a wife of David.

chapters.n: Maachah’s sons founded more towns. Caleb’s daughter Achsah is mentioned—probably reflecting the famous Achsah, daughter of the later Caleb who received springs as a gift.
Another branch of Caleb’s descendants through Hur is introduced, connected with Kirjath-jearim, where the ark of the covenant later rested.
Salma is named as the “father,” or founder, of Bethlehem—the town of David, and later the birthplace of Jesus.
Shobal’s descendants include half of a clan called the Manahethites.

f.g: Meaning “the seer”; perhaps the same as Reaiah in 1 Chronicles 4:2.

chapters.n: The families of Kirjath-jearim spread to nearby towns Zorah and Eshtaol—the home region of Samson.
Salma’s descendants include the people of Bethlehem and Netophah, a village that later produced some of David’s mighty men.
The chapter ends with clans of scribes and the Kenites, a non-Israelite people associated with Moses’ father-in-law. Rechab’s descendants were later praised by Jeremiah for their faithfulness.
David’s sons born during his seven years in Hebron are listed by mother. This royal family line is the center of the chronicler’s hope for Israel.

f.g: Called Chileab in 2 Samuel 3:3; not the prophet Daniel.

chapters.n: Absalom and Adonijah are named—both later tried to seize David’s throne. Absalom’s mother was a foreign princess, a marriage that sealed an alliance with Geshur.
David’s fifth and sixth sons, about whom little else is known.

f.g: Only Eglah is called “his wife,” though all these women were David’s wives.

chapters.n: David ruled in Hebron seven and a half years, then thirty-three years in Jerusalem—about forty years in all (about 1010–970 BC).
Four sons were born to Bath-shua (Bathsheba) in Jerusalem, including Nathan and Solomon. Luke traces Jesus’ ancestry through Nathan; Matthew traces it through Solomon.

f.g: Bathsheba; her father Ammiel is called Eliam in 2 Samuel 11:3.

chapters.n: More sons born to David in Jerusalem by other wives.
Nogah and Nepheg, two names not found in the parallel list in 2 Samuel—perhaps sons who died young.

f.g: “Brightness”; found also in 1 Chronicles 14:6 but not in 2 Samuel 5.

chapters.n: The last of nine Jerusalem-born sons. The repeated names (Elishama, Eliphelet) may honor brothers who had died.

f.g: “God is deliverance”; appears twice in this list.

chapters.n: Besides these were sons of David’s concubines and his daughter Tamar, whose tragic story is told in 2 Samuel 13.
The royal line now runs from Solomon through the kings of Judah, father to son—an unbroken chain of David’s house, as God had promised.

f.g: Abijah, also called Abijam in 1 Kings 15:1.

chapters.n: The list continues through Joram, Ahaziah and Joash. Queen Athaliah’s usurpation between Ahaziah and Joash is passed over, since she was not of David’s line.
Next come Amaziah, Azariah (better known as Uzziah) and Jotham—kings of the eighth century BC in the days of Isaiah.

f.g: Also called Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:1; Isaiah 6:1).

chapters.n: Ahaz the unfaithful, Hezekiah the reformer and Manasseh the idolater: three very different kings in three generations.
The line reaches Amon and then Josiah, Judah’s great reforming king.
Josiah’s four sons; three of them ruled Judah in its final years. Shallum is better known as Jehoahaz.

f.g: Jehoahaz, who ruled only three months (2 Kings 23:31; Jeremiah 22:11).
Otherwise unknown; he may have died young.

chapters.n: Jehoiakim’s son Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) was taken to Babylon in 597 BC. The Zedekiah named here may be a different man from King Zedekiah, Josiah’s son.

f.g: Also called Jehoiachin or Coniah.

chapters.n: Even in exile David’s line continues. Jeconiah’s son Salathiel (Shealtiel) appears in the genealogies of Jesus.

f.g: May mean “captive,” describing Jeconiah rather than naming a son.

chapters.n: Jeconiah had more sons in Babylon. Babylonian ration records mention provisions for his sons, confirming they lived there.

f.g: Some scholars connect him with Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah in Ezra 1:8, though this is uncertain.

chapters.n: Zerubbabel, who led the first return from exile and rebuilt the temple, is a grandson of Jeconiah. Elsewhere he is called Shealtiel’s son—perhaps through adoption or levirate marriage.

f.g: A daughter included in the royal line, unusual in such lists.

chapters.n: Zerubbabel had five more sons, whose names express hope: “thought of,” “tent,” “the LORD blesses,” “the LORD is kind,” and “kindness returns.”

f.g: “Kindness (or covenant love) will return”—a hopeful name for a child born after exile.

chapters.n: The line continues past Zerubbabel through Hananiah and several related families. The text here is difficult and may list branches rather than a single line.

f.g: “The LORD has delivered.”

chapters.n: Through Shechaniah and Shemaiah comes Hattush, who returned to Jerusalem with Ezra.
The descendants of Neariah carry the royal line into the Persian period.

f.g: A later descendant named after the great king, not King Hezekiah himself.

chapters.n: The genealogy ends about eight generations after Jeconiah, reaching close to the chronicler’s own time. David’s line has survived exile, keeping alive the hope of the Messiah, the Son of David.

f.g: “Cloud”; some ancient Jewish interpreters linked this name with the Messiah coming on the clouds (Daniel 7:13).

chapters.n: The chronicler returns to Judah’s clans with a quick line of descent from Judah through several generations. These names lead into additional family branches not covered in chapter 2.

f.g: Probably a copying variant for Caleb (Chelubai) in 2:9, since Carmi belonged to Zerah’s line.

chapters.n: These families settled around Zorah in the lowlands west of Jerusalem.

f.g: People of Zorah, Samson’s hometown (Judges 13:2).

chapters.n: The founders of Etam are listed, including a daughter with an unusual name. Etam was later fortified by King Rehoboam.

f.g: A rare woman’s name, perhaps meaning “give shade, you who turn toward me.”

chapters.n: Hur’s descendants founded towns in the Judean hills, and Hur himself is linked with Bethlehem’s founding.
Ashur, founder of Tekoa, had two wives whose sons are listed next.
The sons of Naarah. Haahashtari may be a clan name rather than a personal name.

f.g: Possibly “the Ahashtarite,” a clan with a Persian-sounding name.

chapters.n: The sons of Helah, Ashur’s other wife.

f.g: Means “gift” or “hire.”

chapters.n: More clans of Judah, whose connection to the main line is not spelled out—the chronicler preserves even the names he cannot fully place.

f.g: Ancestor of a clan; the name may mean “thorn.”

chapters.n: Suddenly the list pauses for a story. Jabez was more honorable than his brothers, yet his name sounds like the Hebrew word for “pain,” given because of his difficult birth.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew ‘otsev, “pain” or “sorrow”—a name that could feel like a curse.
More respected, or of better character.

chapters.n: Jabez prays that God will bless him, widen his land, be with him, and keep him from harm so his name would not define his life. God answers. The lesson: no one’s past or label is beyond God’s power to bless.

f.g: Expand my territory; “coast” in the KJV means border or region.

f.w: God granted him that which he requested

chapters.n: The genealogy resumes with the clan of Chelub.

f.g: Another form of the name Caleb, though perhaps a different person.

chapters.n: These families settled at towns like Ir-nahash, “city of the serpent,” possibly a copper-working site.

f.g: “City of the snake” or “city of copper”; location uncertain.

chapters.n: Othniel, Caleb’s nephew, was Israel’s first judge after Joshua, who delivered Israel from oppression and brought forty years of peace.
Joab (not David’s general) founded the “valley of craftsmen,” a community known for skilled work.

f.g: “Craftsmen”; the valley of skilled workers.

chapters.n: The family of Caleb son of Jephunneh—the faithful spy who, with Joshua, trusted God to give Israel the land and received Hebron as his inheritance.
The sons of Jehaleleel, whose names include Ziph, a town in Judah’s wilderness.
The sons of Ezra (an ancestor, not the later scribe), including a daughter named Miriam—the same name as Moses’ sister.

f.g: Here possibly a son or daughter; the Hebrew is unclear. The name is the source of “Mary.”

chapters.n: Mered had a Judahite wife and an Egyptian wife, Bithiah, a daughter of Pharaoh. A foreign princess joined Israel’s family—God’s covenant people have always welcomed outsiders.

f.g: Her name means “daughter of the LORD,” perhaps given after she joined Israel.
“The Jewess,” probably meaning his Judahite wife.

chapters.n: The sons of Hodiah are tied to Keilah, a town David later rescued from the Philistines.
Two more short family lists from Judah.

f.g: “Son of the gracious one.”

chapters.n: Judah’s third son Shelah had descendants who became a guild of linen weavers—Chronicles remembers people by their trades as well as their names.

f.g: Made fine linen cloth, a valued skill.

chapters.n: Some of Shelah’s clans once ruled in Moab. The chronicler notes these are “ancient things”—old records he faithfully preserved.

f.g: These records are very old, a hint that the chronicler drew on earlier sources.

chapters.n: These families were royal potters and gardeners, living on crown estates to work for the king.

f.g: Possibly place names, Netaim and Gederah, or simply farmland and enclosures.

chapters.n: The tribe of Simeon is introduced next. Simeon’s land lay within Judah’s territory in the south, and over time the two tribes largely merged.
Simeon’s line continues through Shaul’s descendants.

f.g: “Sweet smell”; a name also found among Ishmael’s sons (1 Chronicles 1:29).

chapters.n: Three more generations lead to Shimei.

f.g: Related to the name Zacchaeus, meaning “remembered.”

chapters.n: Shimei had a large family, but Simeon as a whole stayed small compared with Judah—fulfilling Jacob’s words that Simeon would be scattered.

f.w: neither did all their family multiply

chapters.n: Simeon’s towns in the Negev, the dry southern region, begin with Beer-sheba, famous from the stories of Abraham and Isaac.
More of Simeon’s southern towns.

f.g: Called Balah in Joshua 19:3.

chapters.n: These towns include Hormah, site of an early victory, and Ziklag, which later became David’s base while fleeing Saul.
Simeon held these towns until David’s reign, when they apparently came under Judah’s control.

f.g: Until David’s time, when Judah absorbed much of Simeon’s territory.

chapters.n: Simeon also held five villages, including Rimmon and Ashan.
The chronicler notes that these settlements, together with their surrounding villages, were Simeon’s officially recorded homes.

f.g: Dwelling places.

chapters.n: A list of Simeonite clan leaders begins.

f.g: Not King Amaziah; a clan leader of Simeon.

chapters.n: More leaders, several traced back four generations.

f.g: A common name; not the king of Israel.

chapters.n: Still more Simeonite leaders, among them Jaakobah, a form of Jacob.

f.g: A form of the name Jacob.

chapters.n: Ziza’s ancestry is traced back five generations, showing the care taken to record family lines.

f.g: A leader of Simeon; the name may mean “abundance.”

chapters.n: These men were leaders of their clans, and their families grew so large that they needed more land.

f.g: Clan chiefs or family heads.

chapters.n: Looking for grazing land, they moved toward Gedor.

f.g: Possibly to be read “Gerar,” a region in the southwest near Philistia, as in the Greek translation.

chapters.n: They found rich, peaceful pastureland once occupied by descendants of Ham—perhaps Egyptians or Canaanites.

f.g: Peoples descended from Ham, such as Egyptians or Canaanites (1 Chronicles 1:8).

chapters.n: In Hezekiah’s time these Simeonites drove out the residents and settled there. The chronicler records this without approving or condemning it.

f.w: in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah
f.g: About 715–686 BC.
Lived in their place.

chapters.n: Five hundred Simeonites went southeast to the hills of Seir, the region of Edom.

f.g: The mountainous region of Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: There they defeated the last surviving Amalekites, Israel’s ancient enemies, and settled in their place.

f.w: the rest of the Amalekites that were escaped

chapters.n: Reuben was Jacob’s firstborn, but he lost the birthright after sleeping with his father’s concubine. The double inheritance of the firstborn went to Joseph’s sons instead.

f.w: his birthright was given unto the sons of Joseph

chapters.n: The chronicler explains a key distinction: Judah became the royal tribe that produced kings, but the birthright belonged to Joseph. Both roles matter in God’s plan for Israel.

f.w: of him came the chief ruler

chapters.n: Reuben’s four sons, founders of Reubenite clans, are named.

f.w: Hanoch, and Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi

chapters.n: A line of Reubenite descendants through Joel, whose link to Reuben’s sons is not given.

f.g: A Reubenite; not the Gog of Ezekiel’s prophecy (Ezekiel 38).

chapters.n: The line continues; one descendant is even named Baal, a sign of Canaanite influence in the family.

f.g: “Lord” or “master”—also the name of the Canaanite storm god.

chapters.n: Beerah, a Reubenite chief, was taken captive by Assyria’s King Tiglath-pileser III around 732 BC.

f.g: Tiglath-pileser III, king of Assyria about 745–727 BC.

chapters.n: Other Reubenite clan leaders are listed according to the official family records.

f.w: the genealogy of their generations was reckoned
f.g: When the family records were officially recorded.

chapters.n: Bela’s clan lived around Aroer, Nebo and Baal-meon, towns east of the Dead Sea in the former lands of Sihon.
Their herds grew so large that they spread east toward the desert stretching to the Euphrates.

f.g: The fertile highlands east of the Jordan River.

chapters.n: In Saul’s day the Reubenites defeated the Hagarites, a nomadic people, and took over their land.

f.g: Desert nomads, possibly linked by name with Hagar, mother of Ishmael.

chapters.n: The tribe of Gad lived north of Reuben in Bashan, a region famous for its rich pasture and strong cattle.

f.g: A fertile plateau east of the Sea of Galilee.

chapters.n: The chief leaders of Gad are listed.

f.g: The leading clan head of Gad.

chapters.n: Seven more Gadite family heads.

f.g: The chronicler often totals names to aid memory and accuracy.

chapters.n: Their ancestry is traced back many generations to Buz.

f.g: Here a personal name, the same as the region.

chapters.n: Ahi was head of this Gadite family group.

f.w: chief of the house of their fathers
f.g: Head of the extended family or clan.

chapters.n: Gad lived in Gilead, Bashan and the pasturelands of a region called Sharon east of the Jordan.

f.g: Not the coastal plain of Sharon but an area east of the Jordan with the same name.
Pasturelands around towns.

chapters.n: These records were compiled in the eighth century BC, under Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel—shortly before the northern tribes were exiled.

f.g: Jeroboam II (about 793–753 BC).

chapters.n: The tribes east of the Jordan fielded an army of 44,760 trained warriors.

f.g: A small round shield.

chapters.n: They fought the Hagarites and their allies, desert tribes descended from Ishmael.
This is a key verse for the chronicler’s message: they won because they cried to God in battle and trusted Him. Faith, not military strength, brings victory.

f.w: they cried to God in the battle

f.g: He listened to their plea and answered it.

chapters.n: They captured enormous herds and many captives. The large numbers emphasize how complete the victory was.

f.g: Donkeys.

chapters.n: The battle was “of God,” so the victory was great. Yet the verse ends ominously: they lived there only until the captivity.

f.g: In their place.

chapters.n: The eastern half-tribe of Manasseh grew and spread north to Mount Hermon.

f.g: The Amorite name for Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9).

chapters.n: Manasseh’s leaders are praised as mighty and famous men.

f.g: Strong, brave warriors—also used for men of wealth and standing.

chapters.n: But they turned away from God to worship the gods of the land. Their earlier trust in God gave way to unfaithfulness.

f.g: A strong biblical image: idolatry as unfaithfulness in a marriage covenant with God.

chapters.n: God allowed the Assyrian kings to carry these tribes into exile around 732 BC. These became part of the scattered “lost tribes,” whose gathering the restored Church teaches will be part of the latter days.

f.g: Pul is another name for Tiglath-pileser III; the verse names the same king twice.

chapters.n: This long chapter covers the tribe of Levi, which had no territory but was set apart to serve God. Its placement at the center of the tribal lists shows how important worship was to the chronicler.
Kohath’s four sons; the Kohathites cared for the most holy objects of the tabernacle.
From Amram came Aaron, Moses and Miriam—the family through whom God delivered Israel. Aaron’s sons became the first priests; Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorized fire.
The high priestly line runs through Eleazar to Phinehas, whose zeal earned the promise of an everlasting priesthood.
The line passes through Abishua, Bukki and Uzzi—generations largely unknown outside these lists.
The priestly succession continues. The chronicler is showing that the priesthood was passed down legitimately, generation by generation.

f.g: “Rebellious”; an ancestor in the high priestly line.

chapters.n: Amariah and Ahitub lead to the important figure of Zadok. Interestingly, the high priest Eli and his descendants, from Ithamar’s line, are not included here.

f.g: A name used for more than one man in the priestly line (see verse 11).

chapters.n: Zadok served as high priest under David and anointed Solomon king. His descendants held the high priesthood for centuries.
The line continues from Zadok’s son Ahimaaz.
This Azariah is noted as serving in Solomon’s temple. Some think the note belongs to the Azariah who bravely confronted King Uzziah for trespassing in the temple.

f.g: Served as priest; carried out priestly duties.

chapters.n: The names Amariah and Ahitub repeat, a common pattern as families honored ancestors.
A second Zadok and his son Shallum continue the priestly line toward the end of the monarchy.

f.g: Also called Meshullam (1 Chronicles 9:11).

chapters.n: Hilkiah is the high priest who found the book of the law in the temple during Josiah’s reign.
Seraiah was high priest when Jerusalem fell and was executed by the Babylonians. His son Jehozadak carried the line into exile.

f.g: Also called Jozadak; father of Joshua (Jeshua), the high priest after the return.

chapters.n: The high priestly line goes into Babylonian captivity, but it is not broken. The chronicler says plainly that it was the Lord who sent Judah away—exile was His judgment, not merely Babylon’s power.
The chronicler restarts the list of Levi’s sons, this time to trace the non-priestly Levite families who served as assistants and singers.

f.g: Another spelling of Gershon (verse 1).

chapters.n: Gershom’s two sons founded Levite clans.
Kohath’s sons are repeated here as the start of the Levite family lists.

f.w: Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel

chapters.n: Merari’s two sons complete the three main Levite branches.
Gershom’s line is traced through several generations.

f.g: A common Levite name, appearing in several lines.

chapters.n: Gershom’s descendants continue down to Jeaterai.

f.g: Not the prophet Iddo of 2 Chronicles 9:29.

chapters.n: Kohath’s line leads to Korah, who rebelled against Moses. Yet Korah’s sons did not die with him, and their descendants became temple singers credited with several Psalms.

f.g: Possibly another name for Izhar, Korah’s father (compare verse 38).

chapters.n: Korah’s descendants continue through Elkanah and Ebiasaph.

f.g: Also called Abiasaph (Exodus 6:24).

chapters.n: The line continues with Tahath, Uriel, Uzziah and Shaul.

f.g: A Levite, not the king of the same name.

chapters.n: Another branch through Elkanah.

f.g: “Burden-bearer.”

chapters.n: This Elkanah’s line leads toward the family of the prophet Samuel.

f.g: Also called Zuph (verse 35; 1 Samuel 1:1).

chapters.n: The line reaches Elkanah, Samuel’s father. Chronicles shows that Samuel, though living in Ephraim, was a Levite by descent—helping explain his priestly service.
Samuel’s sons are named. 1 Samuel calls the firstborn Joel; “Vashni” may be a copying slip for “and the second.”

f.g: Probably a misreading of Hebrew “and the second”; 1 Samuel 8:2 names Joel as firstborn.

chapters.n: Merari’s line is traced through several generations.

f.g: A Levite; not the Uzza who touched the ark (1 Chronicles 13:9-10).

chapters.n: The list of Merari’s descendants ends with Asaiah, possibly the Levite leader in David’s day.
David organized Levite musicians for worship once the ark had a permanent home. Music, for the chronicler, is central to temple worship.

f.w: after that the ark had rest
f.g: After the ark was brought to Jerusalem and no longer moved from place to place.

chapters.n: They led sacred music at the tabernacle until Solomon built the temple, then continued in their assigned order there.

f.g: Served in their assigned duties.
The tent of meeting, Israel’s portable sanctuary.

chapters.n: Three choir leaders are now traced to Levi. Heman, from Kohath’s line, was a grandson of Samuel the prophet.

f.g: Samuel.

chapters.n: Heman’s ancestry continues backward through Elkanah and Jeroham.

f.g: Also called Tohu (1 Samuel 1:1) and Nahath (verse 26).

chapters.n: The line continues back through Zuph, whose name was given to the region where Samuel’s family lived.
More of Heman’s ancestors, matching (with variant spellings) the earlier list.

f.g: A Levite ancestor; not the prophet.

chapters.n: The line reaches Korah, linking Heman to the family whose sons became temple singers.
Heman’s line goes all the way back to Israel (Jacob) himself. Listing it upward like this emphasizes his legitimacy to serve.

f.g: Jacob, whose name God changed to Israel.

chapters.n: Asaph, from Gershom’s line, stood at Heman’s right hand. Twelve psalms are attributed to Asaph or his musical guild.

f.g: Asaph’s choir stood on Heman’s right; Ethan’s on his left (verse 44).

chapters.n: Asaph’s ancestry continues backward.

f.g: “My king is the LORD.”

chapters.n: More ancestors of Asaph.

f.g: Perhaps the same as Jeaterai (verse 21).

chapters.n: The list climbs back through Ethan and Zimmah.
Asaph’s line ends at Gershom, son of Levi.

f.g: Asaph represents the Gershonite clan among the musicians.

chapters.n: The Merarite leader Ethan (also called Jeduthun) stood on the left. So all three branches of Levi led the music together.

f.g: Probably the same as Jeduthun (1 Chronicles 16:41; 1 Chronicles 25:1).

chapters.n: Ethan’s ancestry continues back.

f.g: A Levite ancestor, not the later high priest.

chapters.n: More generations in Ethan’s line.

f.g: “Built”; a common name in Levite and post-exilic lists.

chapters.n: Ethan’s line reaches back to Merari, son of Levi.

f.g: Ethan represents the Merarite clan among the musicians.

chapters.n: The other Levites were assigned all the practical work of the sanctuary—every kind of service mattered.
Only Aaron’s descendants offered sacrifices and incense and made atonement for Israel. These rituals pointed forward to Jesus Christ, the great High Priest whose sacrifice brings true atonement.

f.w: to make an atonement for Israel

f.g: The Holy of Holies, entered only by the high priest once a year.

chapters.n: The high priestly line from Aaron is repeated briefly, ending with Ahimaaz in David and Solomon’s time.
The repeated list affirms the line’s continuity.

f.g: “The LORD has shone forth.”

chapters.n: The names lead again to Ahitub, Zadok’s father.
The short list ends with Zadok and Ahimaaz, the priests of the united kingdom.
Now the chronicler lists the Levite towns, beginning with those given to Aaron’s descendants. Levites received towns scattered among all the tribes instead of a territory of their own.

f.g: Settlements or encampments.

chapters.n: The priests received Hebron and its pasturelands in Judah—a city rich in history from Abraham to David.
Hebron’s surrounding fields and villages remained Caleb’s, as Joshua had promised him.

f.w: they gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh

chapters.n: Hebron was also a city of refuge, where someone who killed accidentally could flee for protection until a fair trial. Other priestly towns in Judah are listed.
More priestly towns, including Debir, captured by Othniel.

f.g: Called Holon in Joshua 21:15.

chapters.n: Beth-shemesh is where the ark returned from the Philistines on a cart pulled by cows.
From Benjamin the priests received towns including Anathoth—hometown of the prophet Jeremiah, who came from a priestly family. In all, the priests had thirteen towns.
The other Kohathite families received ten towns, chosen by lot, including some from Manasseh.

f.g: By casting lots, a way of letting God decide the outcome (Proverbs 16:33).

chapters.n: The Gershonites received thirteen towns in the north, from Issachar, Asher, Naphtali and eastern Manasseh.
The Merarites received twelve towns from Reuben, Gad and Zebulun. Together with the others, this totals forty-eight Levite towns.
This was Israel’s gift to the Levites: by spreading God’s servants throughout the land, every tribe had access to people who could teach the law.

f.w: the children of Israel gave to the Levites

chapters.n: A summary note: the towns from Judah, Simeon and Benjamin were assigned by lot and listed by name.

f.w: which are called by their names

chapters.n: The remaining Kohathite families received towns in Ephraim.

f.g: The rest; the remainder.

chapters.n: Shechem, a city of refuge, was where Joshua led Israel in renewing the covenant. Gezer was later given to Solomon by Pharaoh.
Beth-horon was the pass where God helped Joshua rout the Amorites.

f.g: Called Kibzaim in Joshua 21:22.

chapters.n: Aijalon is the valley over which Joshua asked the moon to stand still.
Two towns from western Manasseh complete the Kohathite list.

f.g: Probably Ibleam, a town in the Jezreel region.

chapters.n: The Gershonites received Golan in Bashan, another city of refuge, and Ashtaroth, once the capital of King Og.
Towns in Issachar given to the Gershonites.

f.g: Called Kishion in Joshua 21:28; not the Kedesh in Galilee.

chapters.n: More Gershonite towns in Issachar.

f.g: Called Jarmuth in Joshua 21:29; not Ramoth-gilead.

chapters.n: Towns in Asher along the northern coast, including Abdon.

f.g: Called Mishal in Joshua 21:30.

chapters.n: Two more towns in Asher’s territory.
In Naphtali, the Gershonites received Kedesh in Galilee, another city of refuge.
The Merarites received towns in Zebulun, including Tabor, near the mountain where Deborah and Barak gathered their army.
East of the Jordan, they received Bezer, a city of refuge, and Jahzah, where Israel defeated King Sihon.
Two more towns from Reuben’s territory.
From Gad came Ramoth-gilead, the sixth city of refuge, and Mahanaim, where Jacob saw angels and where David took refuge during Absalom’s revolt.

The list ends with Heshbon, former capital of the Amorite king Sihon, and Jazer. With these, all six cities of refuge have appeared—places of mercy that many see as a type of the refuge we find in Christ.
This chapter briefly covers six northern tribes. It begins with Issachar, whose four sons founded its main clans.

f.g: A later judge of Israel shared this name (Judges 10:1).

chapters.n: Tola’s descendants were numbered in David’s time at 22,600 fighting men. These figures likely come from David’s census records.

f.g: That is; namely.

chapters.n: Uzzi’s family produced five clan leaders.

f.g: Leaders or heads of clans.

chapters.n: These families could field 36,000 soldiers, because large households with many wives and sons made the clan grow quickly.

f.g: Military units drawn from the clans.

chapters.n: Altogether Issachar counted 87,000 fighting men.

f.g: 87,000 (a score is twenty).

chapters.n: Benjamin’s family is sketched briefly here and more fully in chapter 8. The lists of Benjamin’s sons vary somewhat from book to book.
Bela’s five sons headed clans totaling 22,034 warriors.

f.g: Capable fighting men; sometimes also men of wealth and standing.

chapters.n: Becher’s sons include names that match towns in Benjamin, such as Anathoth and Alameth.
Becher’s clan numbered 20,200 fighting men.

f.w: after their genealogy by their generations
f.g: According to their official family records.

chapters.n: Jediael’s descendants include an Ehud, a name famous from the left-handed Benjamite judge.

f.g: Possibly not the judge Ehud son of Gera (Judges 3:15), though the name is the same.

chapters.n: Jediael’s clan numbered 17,200 soldiers ready for battle.

f.w: fit to go out for war
f.g: Of age and able to fight.

chapters.n: A short note naming more families. Since Hushim is elsewhere a son of Dan, many think this verse is all that remains of Dan’s genealogy, which is otherwise missing from Chronicles.

f.g: Means “another”; possibly a substitute for a name.

chapters.n: Naphtali’s genealogy is the shortest of all—just four sons, descended from Bilhah, Rachel’s maid.
Manasseh’s line includes Machir, born to an Aramean secondary wife. Lehi in the Book of Mormon was a descendant of Manasseh.

f.g: An Aramean (Syrian) woman.

chapters.n: Zelophehad had only daughters. Their faith and courage changed Israel’s law so that daughters could inherit when there were no sons.
Machir’s wife Maachah names her sons, continuing Manasseh’s line in Gilead.

f.g: Possibly “separate” or “dung”—names in these lists are not always flattering.

chapters.n: These are the descendants of Gilead, Machir’s son, who gave his name to the region.

f.g: Perhaps the same as the judge Bedan in 1 Samuel 12:11, though this is uncertain.

chapters.n: Gilead’s sister Hammoleketh bore a son Abiezer, ancestor of Gideon the judge.

f.g: Means “the queen”; she may have led her clan.

chapters.n: Shemida’s sons include Shechem, whose family may be linked with the famous city.
Ephraim’s line begins, running through many generations.
Two of Ephraim’s sons were killed while raiding cattle from the native people of Gath—a tragic event otherwise unknown.

f.w: the men of Gath that were born in that land
f.g: Native inhabitants of Gath, a city later belonging to the Philistines.

chapters.n: Ephraim grieved for many days and his family came to comfort him—a tender glimpse of a father’s loss.
Ephraim named a new son Beriah, a name that sounds like “in misfortune,” remembering the family’s sorrow.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew bera‘ah, “in evil” or “in disaster.”

chapters.n: Remarkably, a woman named Sherah is credited with building towns, including the two Beth-horons—a rare note about a woman builder.

f.w: Beth-horon the nether, and the upper
f.g: Lower and Upper Beth-horon, guarding an important pass into the hill country.

chapters.n: Ephraim’s family line continues toward its most famous member.

f.g: Also the name of a Canaanite god of plague.

chapters.n: The generations continue. Elishama was Ephraim’s tribal leader in the wilderness.
The line ends with Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ successor who led Israel into the promised land. His name is the Hebrew form of “Jesus,” meaning “the LORD saves.”

f.g: Nun.
Joshua; the same name as Jesus (Greek Iēsous).

chapters.n: Ephraim’s lands stretched across the central hill country, including Bethel and Shechem.

f.g: Probably a town near Bethel (some manuscripts read “Ayyah”), not the Philistine city.

chapters.n: Manasseh held strong cities along the Jezreel Valley, including Megiddo. These were the lands of Joseph’s descendants.
Asher’s children are listed, including a daughter, Serah, who is also named in Genesis and Numbers.
Beriah’s sons, founders of Asherite clans.
Heber’s family, including another daughter, Shua.

f.g: Another daughter remembered by name.

chapters.n: Japhlet’s sons.

f.g: Possibly linked to the Japhletites near Ephraim’s border (Joshua 16:3).

chapters.n: The sons of Shamer (Shomer).

f.g: Same as Shomer in verse 32.

chapters.n: The sons of Helem, Shamer’s brother.

f.g: Perhaps the same as Hotham in verse 32.

chapters.n: Zophah’s large family begins.

f.g: A name that may be Egyptian in origin.

chapters.n: More of Zophah’s sons.

f.g: Possibly the same as Jether in verse 38.

chapters.n: The sons of Jether, including a Jephunneh—not Caleb’s father.

f.g: An Asherite; not the father of Caleb from Judah.

chapters.n: The sons of Ulla close the list.

f.g: An Asherite clan head otherwise unknown.

chapters.n: Asher’s clan heads were choice warriors, numbering 26,000. Though some tribes were later scattered, the chronicler lovingly preserves their names as part of all Israel.

f.w: choice and mighty men of valour
f.g: Select, outstanding warriors.
Fit for battle.

chapters.n: Benjamin receives a fuller genealogy, because it was the tribe of King Saul and, with Judah, formed the core of the southern kingdom and the community after the exile.
Benjamin’s five sons, listed in birth order. The names differ in places from the lists in Genesis and Numbers, perhaps reflecting clans at different times.

f.g: A Benjamite clan head; not related to the Rephaim giants.

chapters.n: Bela’s sons include Gera, an ancestor name shared by the judge Ehud and by Shimei, who cursed David.
More of Bela’s descendants, among them a Naaman—not the Syrian general healed by Elisha.
The list of Bela’s sons concludes.

f.g: Also called Shupham or Shuppim (Numbers 26:39).

chapters.n: Ehud’s clans lived at Geba but were later relocated to Manahath. The text hints at a migration or conflict it does not explain.

f.g: Moved them, perhaps forcibly, to another place.

chapters.n: Gera led this move, and his line continued through Uzza and Ahihud.

f.g: Probably Gera, who led the relocation.

chapters.n: Shaharaim had children in Moab after divorcing two wives. Ruth’s story shows other contact between Israel and Moab in early times.

f.g: Divorced them.

chapters.n: Shaharaim’s sons by his wife Hodesh in Moab. Some names, like Mesha, match known Moabite names.

f.g: Also the name of a famous Moabite king (2 Kings 3:4), though not the same man.

chapters.n: These sons became family leaders.

f.g: Heads of clans or ancestral houses.

chapters.n: Shaharaim also had sons by his earlier wife Hushim.

f.g: “God has worked”; his family is traced in the next verses.

chapters.n: Elpaal’s son Shamed built Ono and Lod, towns in the coastal lowlands. Lod became Lydda in the New Testament, where Peter healed Aeneas.
Beriah and Shema led the people of Aijalon and drove out Gath’s inhabitants—perhaps an echo of conflict reported in chapter 7.

f.w: drove away the inhabitants of Gath

chapters.n: More Benjamite families begin to be listed by their founders.

f.g: His sons are listed in verses 22–25.

chapters.n: The list continues; Arad is also the name of a town in the Negev.

f.g: A personal name here; also a Canaanite city in the south (Numbers 21:1).

chapters.n: These are the sons of Beriah.

f.g: Beriah of Aijalon, from verse 13.

chapters.n: The sons of Elpaal begin to be listed.

f.g: A short form of Hezekiah, “the LORD strengthens.”

chapters.n: These are Elpaal’s sons, Benjamite family heads.

f.g: Elpaal of verses 11–12.

chapters.n: The sons of Shimhi begin.

f.g: “Remembered”; a name that appears several times in this chapter.

chapters.n: More of Shimhi’s sons, two of whose names honor God (Eli-).

f.g: “My God is God.”

chapters.n: These are the sons of Shimhi, probably the same as Shema of verse 13.

f.g: Possibly Shema of verse 13.

chapters.n: The sons of Shashak begin.

f.g: A common name meaning “companion” or “associate.”

chapters.n: More sons of Shashak.

f.g: “Gracious.”

chapters.n: Antothijah’s name may link him to the town of Anathoth.

f.g: Perhaps “the Anathothite,” from the town of Anathoth.

chapters.n: These were the sons of Shashak, Benjamite clan leaders.

f.g: “Face of God”; also the place where Jacob wrestled (Genesis 32:30).

chapters.n: The sons of Jeroham begin, including a man named Athaliah—a name more famous for a wicked queen.

f.g: Here a man’s name; the name was used for both men and women.

chapters.n: Jeroham’s sons complete this list of Benjamite families.
These clan heads lived in Jerusalem, which lay on the border of Benjamin and Judah.
The chronicler turns to Gibeon, a town northwest of Jerusalem, where Saul’s ancestors lived. The Gibeonites had tricked Joshua into a peace treaty long before.

f.g: The founder or leading clan head of Gibeon, named Jeiel in 1 Chronicles 9:35.

chapters.n: His sons include Kish, a family name in Saul’s line.

f.g: A Kish, uncle of Saul’s father Kish; family names often repeated.

chapters.n: More sons of Gibeon’s founder.

f.g: Called Zechariah in 1 Chronicles 9:37.

chapters.n: Mikloth’s family lived near their relatives in Jerusalem.

f.g: Near or alongside them.

chapters.n: Here is Saul’s family tree: from Ner and Kish to Saul and his sons. Esh-baal is better known as Ish-bosheth, who briefly ruled after Saul.

f.g: “Man of Baal,” meaning “man of the Lord”; later writers changed it to Ish-bosheth, “man of shame.”

chapters.n: Jonathan’s son Merib-baal is Mephibosheth, the lame prince whom David treated with kindness for Jonathan’s sake.

f.g: Called Mephibosheth in 2 Samuel, again replacing “baal” with “bosheth” (shame).
Called Mica in 2 Samuel 9:12.

chapters.n: Saul’s line continued through Micah’s four sons.
The line of Saul continues for several more generations, showing that his house survived.

f.g: Also the name of a Benjamite town near Jerusalem (Ezra 2:24).

chapters.n: The descendants continue through Moza, Binea and others.

f.g: His six sons are named in the next verse.

chapters.n: Azel’s six sons are listed—about twelve generations after Saul.
The family of Azel’s brother Eshek is listed too.

f.g: Mentioned only here.

chapters.n: Ulam’s sons were brave archers with many descendants. Benjamin was known for skilled marksmen; centuries later the apostle Paul proudly called himself a Benjamite.

f.w: All these are of the sons of Benjamin

chapters.n: This verse wraps up the tribal genealogies and bluntly states why Judah went into exile: unfaithfulness. Yet the careful records show that God’s people still had an identity worth preserving.

f.g: Registered by family records, establishing each person’s tribe and place.

f.w: carried away to Babylon for their transgression

chapters.n: The chronicler now lists those who resettled their towns after the exile: lay Israelites, priests, Levites, and temple servants. Much of this list parallels Nehemiah 11.

f.g: “Those given”—temple servants who assisted the Levites.

chapters.n: Families from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh lived in Jerusalem. Including northern tribes shows the chronicler’s hope that “all Israel” belongs together.
Uthai led a family from Judah’s Pharez line—the same line as David.
The Shilonites, probably descendants of Judah’s son Shelah, are represented by Asaiah.

f.g: Probably “Shelanites,” descendants of Shelah (Numbers 26:20), rather than people from Shiloh.

chapters.n: Zerah’s descendants, the third branch of Judah, numbered 690. All three branches of Judah were represented in the restored city.
Benjamite families in Jerusalem are listed with their ancestry.
More Benjamite family heads, each identified by several generations of ancestors.

f.g: A very common name after the exile, meaning “restored” or “recompensed.”

chapters.n: The Benjamites in Jerusalem numbered 956 family heads and relatives.

f.g: Leading family heads.

chapters.n: The priestly families begin with Jedaiah and Jehoiarib, names that match two of the twenty-four priestly divisions David organized.
Azariah, descended from Zadok, was the chief officer of the temple—showing the high priestly line continued after exile.

f.w: the ruler of the house of God
f.g: Chief officer or overseer of the temple.

chapters.n: Other priests are listed from the families of Pashur and Immer, both known from Jeremiah’s time.
There were 1,760 priests—capable men ready to serve in God’s house.

f.g: Strong, capable men, fit for demanding temple service.

chapters.n: The Levites begin with Shemaiah of Merari’s branch.
Mattaniah, a descendant of Asaph, led the thanksgiving in worship after the return.
Obadiah, a descendant of Jeduthun, and Berechiah, who lived near Netophah, were also Levite musicians.

f.g: People of Netophah, a village near Bethlehem where many Levite singers lived (Nehemiah 12:28).

chapters.n: The gatekeepers are named, led by Shallum.

f.g: Gatekeepers or doorkeepers, not carriers.

chapters.n: Shallum’s family had long guarded the King’s Gate on the east side of the temple.

f.g: Until now; up to this time.

chapters.n: These Korahite gatekeepers carried on a duty their ancestors had performed since the wilderness tabernacle—guarding the entrance to God’s dwelling.

f.g: Here meaning the camp of Israel around the tabernacle.

chapters.n: Phinehas once supervised these guards, and “the LORD was with him”—a blessing the chronicler hopes for every faithful servant.
Zechariah guarded the entrance of the tent of meeting in David’s time.
There were 212 gatekeepers, registered in their villages. Their roles traced back to arrangements made by David and Samuel.

f.g: An older title for a prophet (1 Samuel 9:9).
In their assigned, trusted position.

chapters.n: These families supervised the temple gates in rotating shifts.

f.g: In shifts or watches.

chapters.n: Gatekeepers were stationed on all four sides of the temple.
Relatives from the villages came in to serve week-long shifts, rotating regularly.

f.g: Every seven days—a weekly rotation, like the priests’ courses (Luke 1:8-9).

chapters.n: Four chief gatekeepers held permanent positions and oversaw the storerooms and treasuries.

f.g: Storerooms for offerings, tithes and sacred items.

chapters.n: They lived around the temple and opened its doors every morning—a faithful daily duty.

f.g: They were responsible for guarding it.

chapters.n: Some kept track of the sacred vessels, counting them carefully as they were brought in and out.

f.g: By count; by number.

chapters.n: Others managed temple supplies: flour, wine, oil, incense and spices for offerings.

f.g: A fragrant resin burned as incense.

chapters.n: Only priests mixed the sacred anointing oil and incense, as the law of Moses required.

f.w: made the ointment of the spices

chapters.n: Mattithiah was in charge of baking the flat cakes for grain offerings.

f.w: the things that were made in the pans
f.g: Baked grain offerings (Leviticus 2:5; 1 Chronicles 23:29).

chapters.n: Kohathites prepared the showbread each Sabbath—twelve loaves set before the Lord, one for each tribe.

f.g: “Bread of the Presence,” twelve loaves kept on a table in the holy place.

chapters.n: The Levite musicians lived in temple rooms and were freed from other duties, because they served day and night.
These Levite family heads lived in Jerusalem.

f.g: Living near the temple allowed them to serve continually.

chapters.n: The chronicler repeats Saul’s family tree from chapter 8, here as a bridge into the story of Saul’s death in chapter 10.
Jehiel’s sons, now including Ner, Saul’s grandfather.

f.g: Saul’s grandfather; also the father of Abner, Saul’s general (1 Samuel 14:50).

chapters.n: The rest of Jehiel’s sons, including Mikloth.

f.g: Called Zacher in 1 Chronicles 8:31.

chapters.n: Mikloth’s family lived in Jerusalem near their relatives.

f.g: Called Shimeah in 1 Chronicles 8:32.

chapters.n: Saul and his sons are named again, preparing the reader for their deaths at Mount Gilboa.
Jonathan’s son Merib-baal (Mephibosheth) and grandson Micah carried Jonathan’s line forward.
Micah’s four sons.

f.g: Called Tarea in 1 Chronicles 8:35.

chapters.n: Saul’s line continues through several generations.

f.g: Called Jehoadah in 1 Chronicles 8:36.

chapters.n: The descendants continue to Azel.

f.g: Called Rapha in 1 Chronicles 8:37.

chapters.n: Azel’s six sons end the list. The chronicler is now ready to begin his narrative with Saul’s fall and David’s rise.
The chronicler’s story begins not with Saul’s rise but with his fall. Israel is routed by the Philistines on Mount Gilboa, about 1010 BC—setting the stage for David.

f.g: A ridge on the southeast edge of the Jezreel Valley in northern Israel.

chapters.n: Saul’s sons, including the noble Jonathan, David’s dearest friend, are killed in the battle.

f.g: Pursued closely.

chapters.n: The fighting turns against Saul, and enemy archers badly wound him.

f.g: Went badly for Saul; pressed hard against him.

chapters.n: Fearing torture and mockery by the Philistines, Saul asks his armor-bearer to kill him. When he refuses, Saul falls on his own sword—a tragic end for Israel’s first king.

f.g: A scornful term for the Philistines, who were outside God’s covenant.
Mock or torment me.

chapters.n: The armor-bearer, loyal to the end, takes his own life as well.
Saul and his sons die together. “All his house” here means his royal dynasty effectively ended, though one son, Ish-bosheth, briefly ruled afterward.
Seeing the army’s collapse, Israelites in the valley abandon their towns, and the Philistines occupy them. Saul’s defeat leaves the nation exposed.

f.g: Abandoned their towns.

chapters.n: The next day, Philistines looting the battlefield find the bodies of Saul and his sons.

f.g: To take armor and valuables from the dead, a common practice after battle.

chapters.n: They cut off Saul’s head and send news of their victory to their idols and people, treating it as a triumph of their gods over Israel’s God.

f.g: Announce the victory in their temples, as if thanking their gods.

chapters.n: Saul’s armor is placed in a pagan temple and his head hung in Dagon’s temple—a deep humiliation. Earlier, the ark had humbled Dagon in his own temple.

f.g: A grain or fertility god worshipped by the Philistines.

chapters.n: The people of Jabesh-gilead hear what has happened. Saul had rescued their town at the start of his reign, and they had not forgotten.
Their bravest men recover the bodies and give them an honorable burial, fasting for a week. Their loyalty and gratitude are a quiet bright spot in a dark chapter.

f.g: A sign of deep mourning.

chapters.n: The chronicler explains why Saul died: he was unfaithful to the Lord, disobeyed His word, and even consulted a medium. This is the key lesson of the chapter.

f.w: the word of the LORD, which he kept not
one that had a familiar spirit
f.g: A medium who claimed to call up the dead—the witch of Endor.

chapters.n: Saul did not seek the Lord, so the Lord turned the kingdom to David. The chronicler’s point is clear: blessing comes from seeking God, and the throne is God’s to give.

f.g: 1 Samuel 28:6 says Saul did ask but received no answer; the chronicler means he did not truly seek God in faith and obedience.

chapters.n: All Israel comes to David at Hebron, claiming him as family. The chronicler skips the seven years of civil war in 2 Samuel to emphasize a united people choosing God’s king.

f.w: we are thy bone and thy flesh
f.g: We are your own family and kin.

chapters.n: The people recall that David had already led Israel in battle under Saul, and that God had called him to be a shepherd-ruler over His people. The shepherd image points ahead to Christ, the Good Shepherd.

f.g: Led the army out to battle and brought it home; a phrase for military leadership.

f.w: Thou shalt feed my people Israel

chapters.n: The elders make a covenant with David before the Lord and anoint him king, fulfilling what God had revealed through Samuel years before.

f.w: according to the word of the LORD by Samuel

f.g: Poured oil on his head; “Messiah” and “Christ” both mean “anointed one.”

chapters.n: David leads the united army against Jerusalem, then a Jebusite city called Jebus, on the border between Judah and Benjamin.
The Jebusites mock David, confident in their strong walls. But David captures the fortress of Zion, which becomes “the city of David.” Zion later becomes a name for God’s holy people and dwelling.

f.g: The fortress on the southeastern hill of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: David offers command of the army to whoever leads the attack. Joab goes first and wins the post he will hold for most of David’s reign.
David makes the fortress his home, and it is named after him. Jerusalem becomes Israel’s capital, neutral ground between the northern and southern tribes.

f.g: Originally the small fortified hill of Zion, later expanded.

chapters.n: David builds up the city from the Millo, and Joab restores the rest.

f.g: Probably “the filling”—terraces or earthworks supporting buildings on the hillside.

chapters.n: David’s power steadily grows because the Lord of hosts is with him—the chronicler’s key explanation for every success.

f.g: Grew stronger and stronger.
“Hosts” means armies—of heaven and of Israel; a title of God’s power.

chapters.n: The chronicler introduces David’s mighty men, who supported him in becoming king as the Lord had promised. Great leaders depend on faithful helpers.
Jashobeam, chief of the officers, killed three hundred enemies at one time. The parallel in 2 Samuel gives eight hundred—a likely copying difference in one text.

f.g: Called Josheb-basshebeth in 2 Samuel 23:8.

chapters.n: Eleazar was one of David’s top three warriors.

f.g: An elite group of David’s three greatest warriors.

chapters.n: At Pas-dammim, the army fled from the Philistines in a barley field—but Eleazar stood with David.

f.g: Also called Ephes-dammim, where David fought Goliath (1 Samuel 17:1).
A plot or field.

chapters.n: They held the field and struck down the Philistines. The chronicler credits the Lord: He saved them with a great victory.

f.w: the LORD saved them by a great deliverance

chapters.n: Three warriors join David at the cave of Adullam while the Philistines camp in the valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem.

f.g: A valley southwest of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: David is in his stronghold while a Philistine garrison holds his hometown of Bethlehem.

f.g: The stronghold or fortress.

chapters.n: Homesick and thirsty, David wishes aloud for water from Bethlehem’s well—a passing longing, not a command.
The three warriors break through enemy lines to bring him the water. Deeply moved, David refuses to drink it and pours it out as an offering to the Lord.

f.w: poured it out to the LORD
f.g: A drink offering: giving to God something too precious for himself.

chapters.n: David says the water is like the blood of men who risked their lives—too sacred to drink. His response honors their sacrifice and shows a leader who would not take loyalty for granted.

f.g: Danger; risk.

chapters.n: Abishai, Joab’s brother, led a second group of three and became famous for killing three hundred enemies.
Abishai was the most honored of his group and its captain, though not equal to the first three.

f.w: attained not to the first three
f.g: Did not rank with the top three warriors.

chapters.n: Benaiah performed heroic deeds: he killed two of Moab’s champion warriors and a lion in a pit on a snowy day.

f.g: Hebrew ’ari’el—fierce champions, or possibly “sons of Ariel.”

chapters.n: He faced a giant Egyptian, about seven and a half feet tall, with only a staff—then snatched the Egyptian’s spear and killed him with it. The scene echoes David and Goliath.

f.g: About 7½ feet (2.3 m).

f.w: a spear like a weaver's beam

chapters.n: Benaiah’s exploits earned him fame like the three mighty men.

f.g: Was famous; had a reputation.

chapters.n: Though honored among the Thirty, Benaiah was not one of the top three. David made him head of his bodyguard; later he commanded Solomon’s army.
The list of the Thirty begins with Asahel, Joab’s swift-footed brother, killed by Abner. This Elhanan is different from the one who killed Goliath’s brother.
More of David’s warriors, identified by hometown or clan.

f.g: Called Shammah the Harodite in 2 Samuel 23:25.

chapters.n: Ira came from Tekoa and Abi-ezer from Anathoth—both towns near Jerusalem.

f.g: From Tekoa, south of Bethlehem.
From Anathoth, Jeremiah’s later hometown.

chapters.n: Sibbecai later killed a Philistine giant.
Two warriors from Netophah near Bethlehem.
Some of David’s men came from Benjamin, Saul’s own tribe—a sign that David drew loyalty from across Israel.

f.g: Saul’s hometown in Benjamin.
From Pirathon in Ephraim (Judges 12:15).

chapters.n: More warriors, from the region of Mount Gaash in Ephraim and from the Jordan Valley.
Azmaveth and Eliahba are listed.

f.g: From Shaalbim, a town in Dan’s territory.

chapters.n: The list includes a son of Shage from the hill country.

f.g: Possibly “mountaineer,” someone from the hill country.

chapters.n: Two more of the Thirty.

f.g: Called Eliphelet son of Ahasbai in 2 Samuel 23:34.

chapters.n: Hepher and Ahijah are named.

f.g: Meaning uncertain; possibly “a certain one,” or a town name.

chapters.n: Hezro came from Carmel in Judah, Abigail’s home region.

f.g: From Carmel in Judah, not Mount Carmel.

chapters.n: Joel and Mibhar continue the list.

f.g: Possibly “the Hagrite,” from a desert people (1 Chronicles 5:10).

chapters.n: Zelek was an Ammonite—one of several foreigners who served David faithfully. Naharai carried Joab’s armor.

f.g: A foreigner among David’s elite, showing loyalty mattered more than ancestry.
A soldier who carried a commander’s weapons and shield.

chapters.n: Two Ithrites, from a clan of Kirjath-jearim.
Uriah the Hittite appears among David’s loyal heroes. Chronicles does not retell David’s sin with Bathsheba, but his name here quietly recalls it.
From here the list goes beyond 2 Samuel, adding warriors from east of the Jordan. Adina led thirty Reubenites.

f.g: From the tribe of Reuben, east of the Jordan.

chapters.n: More warriors, including Joshaphat the Mithnite.

f.g: Meaning uncertain; perhaps from an unknown town.

chapters.n: Uzzia came from Ashtaroth and the sons of Hothan from Aroer, both east of the Jordan.

f.g: From Ashtaroth in Bashan.
From Aroer, on the Arnon River.

chapters.n: Two brothers from Tiz, an unknown town.

f.g: From Tiz, location unknown.

chapters.n: Ithmah was a Moabite—another foreigner in David’s service. David’s own great-grandmother Ruth was from Moab.
The list of mighty men closes. These loyal companions from many tribes and even other nations helped build David’s kingdom.

f.g: Possibly from Zobah, an Aramean kingdom.

chapters.n: The chronicler steps back in time to show how warriors joined David even while he was hiding from Saul at Ziklag, a Philistine-granted town. Support for God’s chosen king grew steadily.

f.g: Stayed in hiding; lived in restricted circumstances.

chapters.n: The first to come were ambidextrous archers and slingers from Benjamin—Saul’s own tribe. Even Saul’s relatives recognized that God was with David.

f.w: both the right hand and the left

f.g: Saul’s fellow tribesmen and possibly relatives.

chapters.n: Their leaders are named, some from Saul’s hometown of Gibeah and from Anathoth.

f.g: From Gibeah, Saul’s capital.

chapters.n: Ismaiah from Gibeon was a leader among the Thirty.

f.g: David’s elite band of warriors (1 Chronicles 11:10-47).

chapters.n: More Benjamite warriors who joined David.

f.g: Possibly from a clan or place called Hariph (Nehemiah 7:24).

chapters.n: These were Korahites—Levites descended from Korah, perhaps living among Benjamin—who also came to David.

f.g: Korahites, descendants of Korah the Levite (1 Chronicles 9:19).

chapters.n: Two sons of Jeroham from Gedor complete the Benjamite list.

f.g: A town, perhaps in Benjamin or Judah.

chapters.n: Gadite warriors from east of the Jordan joined David in the wilderness. They are described with vivid images: faces like lions and feet as swift as gazelles.

f.g: David’s stronghold in the wilderness.
Gazelles or deer.

chapters.n: The Gadite leaders are listed in order of rank.

f.g: First in rank among the Gadite captains.

chapters.n: The fourth and fifth Gadite captains.

f.g: Meaning possibly “fatness” or “strength.”

chapters.n: The sixth and seventh captains.

f.g: “My God is God.”

chapters.n: The eighth and ninth captains.

f.g: “God has given.”

chapters.n: The tenth and eleventh captains complete the list.

f.g: A Gadite captain mentioned only here.

chapters.n: These Gadites became army commanders; even the least of them could lead a hundred, the greatest a thousand.

f.w: one of the least was over an hundred
f.g: Or, “one of them could stand against a hundred”—the Hebrew can read either way.

chapters.n: They crossed the Jordan in spring flood season—a dangerous feat—and drove off enemies on both sides of the valley.

f.g: Nisan (March–April), when snowmelt swelled the Jordan.

chapters.n: Men from Benjamin and Judah also came to David’s stronghold.

f.g: Men from both David’s tribe and Saul’s.

chapters.n: David wisely tests their motives: if you come in peace, I will welcome you with all my heart; if you come to betray me, let God judge you.

f.w: mine heart shall be knit unto you
f.g: I will be bound to you in loyal friendship.
Judge and punish it.

chapters.n: The Spirit inspires Amasai to pledge loyalty in poetic words: “We are yours, David… peace to you, for your God helps you.” David welcomes them as officers.

f.g: Literally “the Spirit clothed Amasai”—filling him to speak inspired words.

chapters.n: Some men of Manasseh defected to David when he marched with the Philistines toward Saul’s final battle. The Philistine rulers distrusted David and sent him away—sparing him from fighting Israel.

f.w: the lords of the Philistines upon advisement sent him away

f.g: After consulting together.

chapters.n: On his way back to Ziklag, seven commanders from Manasseh joined him.

f.g: Officers each commanding a large military unit.

chapters.n: They helped David fight the Amalekite raiders who had burned Ziklag and taken his family.

f.g: The raiding party—the Amalekites.

chapters.n: Day after day more people came until David’s force was like the army of God—a hint that heaven was behind this growing movement.

f.g: An idiom for something very great; also suggests divine support.

chapters.n: Now the chronicler lists the warriors who came to Hebron to make David king, as the Lord had promised.

f.w: according to the word of the LORD

chapters.n: Judah sent 6,800 armed men.

f.g: Heavily armed infantry.

chapters.n: Simeon sent 7,100 warriors.

f.g: A small southern tribe closely tied to Judah.

chapters.n: Even the Levites, normally temple servants, sent 4,600 men.

f.g: Levites were not usually counted for war (Numbers 1:47-49); here they show support for David.

chapters.n: Jehoiada led the priestly descendants of Aaron, with 3,700 men.

f.g: Descendants of Aaron—the priestly families.

chapters.n: Zadok, a brave young man, came with twenty-two family commanders. He would later become David’s high priest.
Only 3,000 came from Benjamin, since most of Saul’s tribe had remained loyal to his house until then.

f.w: kept the ward of the house of Saul
f.g: Remained loyal to and guarded Saul’s family’s interests.

chapters.n: Ephraim sent 20,800 renowned warriors.

f.w: famous throughout the house of their fathers
f.g: Well known in their clans.

chapters.n: The western half-tribe of Manasseh sent 18,000, each one named and chosen for the task.

f.g: Specifically designated by name.

chapters.n: Issachar’s leaders were valued for wisdom: they “understood the times” and knew what Israel should do. Discernment can be as valuable as strength.

f.g: Insight into current events and what the moment required.

chapters.n: Zebulun sent 50,000 skilled soldiers who were completely loyal—“not of double heart.”

f.g: Stay in battle formation; disciplined.
Single-minded; wholehearted in loyalty.

chapters.n: Naphtali sent a thousand officers with 37,000 men.

f.g: A northern tribe around the Sea of Galilee.

chapters.n: Dan sent 28,600 skilled fighters.

f.g: Members of the tribe of Dan, by now mostly in the far north (Judges 18).

chapters.n: Asher sent 40,000 trained soldiers.

f.g: A tribe along the northern Mediterranean coast.

chapters.n: The tribes east of the Jordan sent 120,000. The large numbers stress that the whole nation, near and far, embraced David.

f.w: on the other side of Jordan
f.g: East of the Jordan River.

chapters.n: All these came “with a perfect heart”—wholehearted—to make David king, and all Israel was of one mind. Unity around God’s chosen leader is the chronicler’s ideal.

f.g: A whole, undivided, sincere heart.

chapters.n: They feasted with David for three days, supplied by their fellow Israelites.

f.g: A covenant celebration meal, sealing the new relationship.

chapters.n: Even the far northern tribes sent food on every kind of animal. The chapter ends with joy—what unity under God’s king brings.

f.g: Pressed fig cakes, a durable food for travel.

chapters.n: As one of his first acts as king, David consults all his military leaders. He wants the whole nation involved in his plan.

f.g: Took counsel; sought advice.

chapters.n: David proposes gathering all Israel, including priests and Levites, but only “if it be of the LORD.” He seeks both the people’s agreement and God’s will.

f.w: that it be of the LORD our God

f.g: Pasturelands around the towns.

chapters.n: His goal: bring back the ark of the covenant, which had been neglected during Saul’s reign. For the chronicler, restoring true worship is the first priority of a good king.

f.g: The sacred chest holding the tablets of the law, symbol of God’s presence.

f.w: we inquired not at it in the days of Saul

chapters.n: Everyone agrees—the plan seems right to all the people.

f.w: the thing was right in the eyes of all the people
f.g: Popular agreement, though as the story shows, method matters as well as motive.

chapters.n: David gathers Israel from its southern border with Egypt to Hamath in the far north to bring the ark from Kirjath-jearim, where it had rested for about twenty years or more.

f.g: A stream or branch of the Nile region marking Israel’s southwest border.

chapters.n: The ark is called by the Lord’s name, the One enthroned between the cherubim. It represented God’s throne on earth.

f.g: An older name for Kirjath-jearim (Joshua 15:9).

chapters.n: They place the ark on a new cart—the way the Philistines had moved it—rather than having Levites carry it on poles as God’s law required.

f.g: Drove.

chapters.n: David and all Israel celebrate wholeheartedly with music and song. Their joy is real—but their method is still wrong.

f.g: Stringed instruments like small harps or lyres.
Hand drums or tambourines.
Danced and celebrated.

chapters.n: At a threshing floor the oxen stumble, and Uzza reaches out to steady the ark.

f.g: Called Nachon’s threshing floor in 2 Samuel 6:6.

chapters.n: God strikes Uzza dead for touching the ark. The law warned that even Levites who handled the holy objects improperly would die.
