It is a sobering lesson that God’s holy things must be approached His way. Latter-day scripture uses “steadying the ark” as an image for trying to correct God’s work without authority.

f.w: he put his hand to the ark

chapters.n: David is upset that the Lord “broke out” against Uzza. The place is named Perez-uzza, “the breaking out against Uzza.”

f.g: “Breach of Uzza” or “outburst against Uzza.”
Angry or distressed; perhaps both grief and frustration.

chapters.n: David becomes afraid of God and wonders how he can ever bring the ark home. Reverent fear leads him, in time, to learn the right way.
Instead of bringing it into Jerusalem, David leaves the ark at the house of Obed-edom.

f.g: Possibly from Gath-rimmon, a Levite town; he later appears among the Levite gatekeepers (1 Chronicles 26:4).

chapters.n: During the three months the ark stays there, the Lord richly blesses Obed-edom’s household. The same holy presence that brought death to the careless brought blessing to the reverent.

f.w: the LORD blessed the house of Obed-edom

chapters.n: Hiram, king of the wealthy Phoenician port of Tyre, sends cedar and skilled workers to build David a palace—international recognition of David’s new kingdom.

f.g: Prized cedar wood from Lebanon, a mark of royal building.

chapters.n: David understands that his success comes from the Lord, and that God lifted up his kingdom for the sake of His people—not merely for David’s glory.

f.g: A reminder that leadership exists to bless the people, not the leader.

chapters.n: David takes more wives in Jerusalem and has more children. The law warned kings against multiplying wives, and the Book of Mormon and D&C speak to David’s marriages as well.
David’s children born in Jerusalem are named, including Nathan and Solomon, both ancestors of Jesus in the Gospel genealogies.

f.g: Called Shimea in 1 Chronicles 3:5.

chapters.n: More of David’s sons born in Jerusalem.

f.g: “God is salvation.”

chapters.n: Three more sons, matching the list in chapter 3.
The list closes. Beeliada (“the Lord knows”) is called Eliada elsewhere, perhaps because “Baal” (“lord”) later became associated with idolatry.

f.g: “The Lord knows”; called Eliada in 1 Chronicles 3:8 and 2 Samuel 5:16.

chapters.n: When the Philistines hear that David is king over all Israel, they march out to crush him before he grows stronger.

f.g: Came looking for him to attack.

chapters.n: They spread out in the valley of Rephaim, just southwest of Jerusalem.
Unlike Saul, David first asks God for guidance. The Lord tells him to go, promising victory. Seeking the Lord is the secret of David’s success in Chronicles.
David wins and says God burst through his enemies like a flood breaking through a dam. The place is named Baal-perazim, “Lord of breakthroughs.”

f.g: “Lord of breaking through.”

f.w: like the breaking forth of waters
f.g: Like floodwaters bursting out.

chapters.n: The fleeing Philistines leave their idols behind, and David orders them burned, as the law of Moses commanded.
The Philistines regroup and attack again in the same valley.

f.g: Once more.

chapters.n: David asks God again rather than assuming the same plan will work. This time God gives a different strategy: circle around and attack from near the trees.

f.g: He sought fresh guidance for a new situation instead of relying on past success.
Hebrew baka’—probably balsam or poplar trees; the exact tree is uncertain.

chapters.n: The signal will be a sound like marching in the treetops—God’s own army going ahead to fight. David is to move when he hears it.

f.w: a sound of going in the tops of the mulberry trees
God is gone forth before thee

chapters.n: David obeys exactly, and Israel defeats the Philistines from Gibeon all the way to Gezer.

f.w: David therefore did as God commanded him

f.g: Gezer, a city on the edge of the coastal plain.

chapters.n: David’s fame spreads everywhere, and the Lord makes the nations respect and fear him. The chronicler gives God the credit.

f.w: the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations

chapters.n: David builds homes for himself in Jerusalem, but he also prepares a special tent for the ark. Making a place for God is part of building his kingdom.
David has learned from Uzza’s death: only Levites may carry the ark, because God chose them for that service.

f.w: None ought to carry the ark of God but the Levites

chapters.n: Once again David gathers all Israel to Jerusalem to bring the ark to the place he has prepared.

f.g: To its appointed place—the tent in the city of David.

chapters.n: This time David calls the priests and Levites first.

f.g: The priests, descendants of Aaron.

chapters.n: The Levite families are organized under their leaders, beginning with the Kohathites, who were originally assigned to carry the holiest objects.
The Merarites, led by Asaiah, number 220.
The Gershonites, led by Joel, number 130.
Elizaphan’s clan, a branch of the Kohathites, sends 200.

f.g: A Kohathite leader in Moses’ day (Numbers 3:30).

chapters.n: Hebron’s clan, another Kohathite branch, sends eighty.

f.g: Eighty.

chapters.n: Uzziel’s clan, the last of six family groups, sends 112. In all, 862 Levites take part.
David summons both chief priests, Zadok and Abiathar, along with the six Levite leaders.
He tells them to sanctify themselves—to become ritually and spiritually prepared—before carrying the ark.

f.g: Make yourselves holy through cleansing rituals and devotion.

chapters.n: David humbly admits the earlier failure: because we did not seek God “after the due order,” He broke out against us. God’s work must be done in God’s way.

f.g: According to the proper, prescribed pattern.

chapters.n: The priests and Levites prepare themselves as instructed.
This time the Levites carry the ark on their shoulders with poles, exactly as Moses commanded—no cart.

f.g: With the carrying poles in place.

chapters.n: David also organizes musicians to accompany the ark with joyful song and instruments.

f.w: lifting up the voice with joy

chapters.n: Three master musicians are appointed—Heman, Asaph and Ethan—one from each branch of Levi.

f.g: Kushaiah is called Kishi in 1 Chronicles 6:44.

chapters.n: Assistant musicians and gatekeepers of the second rank are named, including Obed-edom, in whose house the ark had rested.

f.g: Of second rank; assistants.

chapters.n: The three leaders play bronze cymbals, probably to keep the rhythm and signal the start of songs.

f.g: Bronze cymbals.

chapters.n: A second group plays lyres set to “Alamoth.”

f.g: A musical term, possibly meaning “young women,” i.e., a higher register or soprano voices.

chapters.n: A third group plays harps set to “the Sheminith” to lead the music.

f.g: A musical term meaning “the eighth,” possibly a lower octave or an eight-stringed instrument.
To lead or direct the music.

chapters.n: Chenaniah, a skilled musician, directs the singing.

f.g: He was in charge of the music; some read “in charge of the carrying.”

chapters.n: Berechiah and Elkanah guard the ark.

f.g: Guards protecting the ark from improper approach.

chapters.n: Priests blow trumpets before the ark, as in Israel’s great processions, and more doorkeepers stand guard.
David, the elders and the army commanders joyfully bring the ark from Obed-edom’s house.
When it is clear that God is helping the Levites carry the ark safely, they offer seven bulls and seven rams in thanksgiving.

f.g: In contrast to the earlier disaster, God now blesses their obedient effort.

chapters.n: David wears a fine linen robe and a linen ephod—simple priestly-style clothing—joining in worship humbly rather than in royal splendor.

f.g: A simple linen garment worn in sacred service.

chapters.n: All Israel brings up the ark with shouts and music. It is one of the most joyful celebrations in the Old Testament.

f.g: Hebrew shofar—a ram’s-horn trumpet.

chapters.n: But Michal, Saul’s daughter and David’s wife, watches from a window and despises David for dancing. Her contempt contrasts with David’s wholehearted joy before the Lord.

f.g: Looked down on him with scorn.

chapters.n: The ark is placed in David’s tent in Jerusalem, and the people offer burnt offerings (wholly given to God) and peace offerings (shared in fellowship).

f.g: Offerings completely burned, symbolizing total dedication to God.
Fellowship offerings, partly eaten by the worshippers in a joyful meal.

chapters.n: David blesses the people in the Lord’s name, acting as a shepherd-king who points his people to God.

f.w: blessed the people in the name of the LORD

chapters.n: He gives every man and woman food for a celebration—bread, meat and a cake of raisins or wine. Everyone shares in the joy.

f.g: Probably a cake of raisins (Hebrew ’ashishah), a festive food.
No one is left out of the celebration.

chapters.n: David appoints Levites to serve continually before the ark: to remember, give thanks and praise God. Worship becomes an ongoing, organized part of national life.

f.g: Or “to invoke” or “to remember”—calling God’s deeds to mind in worship.

f.w: to thank and praise the LORD

chapters.n: Asaph leads, with other Levites on lyres and harps; Asaph sounds the cymbals.
Two priests blow trumpets regularly before the ark.
David gives Asaph a psalm of thanksgiving. What follows weaves together parts of Psalms 105, 96 and 106.

f.g: Gave this psalm to be sung—the first time thanksgiving was formally assigned to Asaph’s choir.

chapters.n: The psalm opens with a call to thank the Lord, pray to Him, and tell others what He has done. Worship naturally leads to witness.

f.w: make known his deeds among the people

chapters.n: Sing to Him and talk about His wonderful works. Praise is meant to fill both songs and conversation.

f.w: talk ye of all his wondrous works

chapters.n: Take pride in God’s holy name; let those who seek Him be glad.

f.w: Glory ye in his holy name
f.g: Boast in, or delight in, God’s name.

chapters.n: Seek the Lord and His strength; seek His face always. Seeking God continually is the heartbeat of the chronicler’s message.
Remember His miracles and the judgments He has spoken. Remembering is a key covenant duty throughout scripture.

f.g: The decisions and laws God has spoken.

chapters.n: The psalm addresses Israel as God’s chosen family, descendants of Jacob.

f.g: Descendants of Israel (Jacob). Psalm 105:6 reads “seed of Abraham.”

chapters.n: The Lord is Israel’s God, yet His authority reaches all the earth.

f.w: his judgments are in all the earth

chapters.n: Always remember His covenant, which He commanded for a thousand generations—that is, forever.

f.w: Be ye mindful always of his covenant

chapters.n: This is the covenant God made with Abraham and swore to Isaac—the Abrahamic covenant that Latter-day Saints believe continues through temple and gospel covenants today.

f.w: the covenant which he made with Abraham

chapters.n: God confirmed this covenant to Jacob as an everlasting decree.
The covenant included the promise of the land of Canaan as Israel’s inheritance.

f.g: Your allotted portion—as though measured out by a surveyor’s line.

chapters.n: God made this promise when the patriarchs were few in number and lived as foreigners in the land.

f.g: Foreigners or resident aliens.

chapters.n: They wandered from nation to nation—Canaan, Egypt and beyond.
God protected them and even rebuked kings for their sake, such as Pharaoh and Abimelech in Abraham’s day.

f.w: he reproved kings for their sakes

chapters.n: God’s warning to the nations: do not touch My anointed ones or harm My prophets. The patriarchs are called prophets because they received revelation.
The psalm now calls all the earth to sing and announce God’s salvation every day. The message reaches beyond Israel to all peoples.

f.w: Sing unto the LORD, all the earth
shew forth from day to day his salvation

chapters.n: Declare His glory among the nations—a missionary vision for God’s people.

f.w: Declare his glory among the heathen

f.g: The nations; non-Israelite peoples.

chapters.n: The Lord is great and worthy of praise and reverence above all supposed gods.
The gods of the nations are mere idols, but the Lord created the heavens. Only the Creator deserves worship.

f.w: all the gods of the people are idols
f.g: Hebrew ’elilim—“nothings” or “worthless things.”

chapters.n: Glory, honor, strength and joy fill God’s presence.

f.w: strength and gladness are in his place
f.g: Psalm 96:6 reads “strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.”

chapters.n: All peoples are invited to give the Lord the glory and strength He deserves.

f.g: Families of the nations.

chapters.n: Bring an offering and come worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness.

f.g: Possibly “in holy attire” or “in the splendor of His holiness.”

chapters.n: All the earth should stand in awe of Him; He holds the world steady.

f.w: the world also shall be stable

chapters.n: Heaven and earth rejoice; let the nations proclaim, “The LORD reigns!”
The sea, the fields and all creation join the celebration. Creation itself is pictured as worshipping its Maker.
The trees sing because the Lord is coming to judge the earth. Christians and Latter-day Saints see this as anticipating Christ’s Second Coming, when He will reign in righteousness.

f.w: he cometh to judge the earth

chapters.n: A familiar refrain: give thanks, for the Lord is good and His mercy lasts forever. This line became a standard chorus in Israel’s worship.

f.g: Hebrew hesed—steadfast, covenant love.

chapters.n: A prayer for deliverance and gathering from among the nations. To the chronicler’s post-exile readers, scattered among other lands, these words would have felt very personal.
The psalm closes with a blessing to the Lord forever, and all the people respond, “Amen!” and praise Him.

f.w: And all the people said, Amen
f.g: “Amen” means “so be it” or “truly,” affirming what was said.

chapters.n: David leaves Asaph and his fellow Levites to serve before the ark daily.

f.g: According to each day’s needs.

chapters.n: Obed-edom and sixty-eight relatives serve as well, with Obed-edom and Hosah as gatekeepers.

f.g: Sixty-eight.

chapters.n: Meanwhile the old tabernacle of Moses stood at Gibeon, where Zadok and the priests continued serving at its altar. Worship took place at two sites until Solomon built the temple.

f.w: the high place that was at Gibeon

chapters.n: The priests at Gibeon offered burnt offerings every morning and evening, as the law of Moses required.
Heman, Jeduthun and other chosen musicians served at Gibeon, giving thanks because the Lord’s mercy endures forever.

f.g: Likely the same as Ethan, the Merarite music leader (1 Chronicles 15:17).

chapters.n: They played trumpets, cymbals and instruments set apart for sacred music. Jeduthun’s sons served as gatekeepers.

f.g: Instruments dedicated to sacred worship.

chapters.n: The celebration ends; everyone goes home, and David returns to bless his own household.

f.w: David returned to bless his house

chapters.n: Now settled in a cedar palace, David is troubled that the ark of God still sits in a tent. He tells Nathan the prophet he wants to build God a house.

f.g: In a tent, under fabric hangings.

chapters.n: Nathan quickly approves, assuming God will bless David’s good intentions. Even prophets sometimes speak from their own judgment before receiving revelation.

f.w: Do all that is in thine heart
f.g: Nathan’s personal opinion, which the Lord soon corrects.

chapters.n: That same night God speaks to Nathan with a different message.

f.w: the word of God came to Nathan

chapters.n: God tells David he is not the one to build the temple. 1 Chronicles 22:8 later explains that David had shed much blood in war.

f.w: Thou shalt not build me an house

chapters.n: God reminds David that since the Exodus He has lived among His people in a moving tent. He has always gone where they went.
God never asked any leader for a cedar house. A temple is a gift God accepts on His terms, not something He needs.

f.g: Shepherd My people—leaders as caretakers.

chapters.n: The Lord reminds David where he came from: a shepherd boy taken from the sheep pens to lead God’s people.

f.g: Sheepfold; pasture enclosure.

chapters.n: God has been with David everywhere, defeated his enemies, and made his name great—promises that echo God’s covenant with Abraham.
God promises to give Israel a secure home where they will be “planted” and no longer oppressed by wicked people.

f.g: Wear them down; oppress them.

chapters.n: Then the great reversal: David wanted to build God a house, but God will build David a “house”—a lasting dynasty. It is a beautiful play on the word “house.”

f.w: the LORD will build thee an house
f.g: “House” here means a royal family line, not a building.

chapters.n: After David dies, God will raise up one of his sons and establish his kingdom.

f.g: Your offspring; your descendant.

chapters.n: This son will build God’s house, and God will establish his throne forever. Solomon built the temple, but the “forever” throne finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the Son of David.

f.w: I will stablish his throne for ever

chapters.n: God will be a Father to David’s son and never withdraw His covenant love as He did from Saul. Hebrews applies this verse to Christ, the Son of God.

f.w: I will be his father, and he shall be my son

f.g: Saul.

chapters.n: God will set David’s son over “mine house and… my kingdom”—showing that Israel’s kingdom is really God’s kingdom. Where 2 Samuel says “thy kingdom,” Chronicles stresses God’s ownership.

f.w: in mine house and in my kingdom

chapters.n: Nathan faithfully delivers the whole revelation to David.

f.g: According to the revelation God gave him.

chapters.n: David goes in and sits before the Lord, overwhelmed: “Who am I…?” His humility is the right response to God’s grace.

f.w: Who am I, O LORD God

f.g: To this point.

chapters.n: David marvels that God, not content with present blessings, has promised his family a future far beyond his lifetime.

f.g: A person of high rank or honor.

chapters.n: David is lost for words: what more can I say? You know me.
David acknowledges that God did all this from His own heart and goodness, not because David earned it.

f.g: By Your own will and gracious purpose.

chapters.n: There is no one like the Lord and no God besides Him.
David praises God for redeeming Israel from Egypt and making them His people—a unique nation shaped by God’s mighty acts.

f.g: To buy back or rescue; used of the Exodus and, ultimately, of Christ’s redemption.
Awe-inspiring power.

chapters.n: God made Israel His own people forever and became their God—the heart of the covenant.
David asks God to do exactly as He promised. Good prayers often take God at His word.
David’s deepest desire is that God’s name, not his own, be honored forever through this covenant.

f.w: that thy name may be magnified for ever

chapters.n: Because God has made this promise, David finds the courage to pray.

f.w: found in his heart to pray
f.g: Found the courage or desire to pray.

chapters.n: David affirms that the Lord is God and has promised this good thing.
David closes by asking God to bless his house forever, confident that whatever God blesses stays blessed.

f.w: thou blessest, O LORD, and it shall be blessed for ever

chapters.n: Right after God’s covenant promise, the chronicler shows it coming true: David subdues the Philistines and takes Gath, the hometown of Goliath.

f.g: One of the five main Philistine cities; 2 Samuel 8:1 calls the conquest “Metheg-ammah.”

chapters.n: David defeats Moab, which becomes a tributary state paying yearly gifts.

f.g: Paid tribute—regular payments from a conquered people.

chapters.n: David defeats Hadarezer of Zobah, a powerful Aramean (Syrian) kingdom, extending his influence toward the Euphrates—close to the borders God promised Abraham.

f.g: Also spelled Hadadezer, “Hadad (a storm god) is help.”

chapters.n: David captures many chariots but disables most of the horses, keeping only enough for a hundred chariots. Israel was not to trust in horses and chariots.

f.g: Hamstrung—cut the leg tendons so the horses could not be used in war.
2 Samuel 8:4 reads 1,700; numbers were easily miscopied.

chapters.n: When the Arameans of Damascus come to help Zobah, David defeats them too.

f.g: The Aramean kingdom centered at Damascus.

chapters.n: David stations troops in Damascus, and the Arameans pay tribute. The chronicler credits the Lord: He gave David victory wherever he went.

f.w: the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went
f.g: Or “the LORD gave David victory wherever he went.”

chapters.n: David brings the gold shields of Hadarezer’s officers to Jerusalem as trophies.

f.g: Ceremonial shields, possibly quivers, a display of wealth.

chapters.n: The huge quantity of bronze captured from Zobah’s cities was later used by Solomon for the temple’s bronze sea, pillars and vessels. David’s wars quietly supply God’s house.

f.g: Called Betah and Berothai in 2 Samuel 8:8.

chapters.n: Tou, king of Hamath to the north, hears of David’s victory over his enemy Hadarezer.

f.g: Called Toi in 2 Samuel 8:9.

chapters.n: Tou sends his son with congratulations and rich gifts, seeking friendship with Israel’s rising king.

f.g: To greet him and ask after his well-being—a diplomatic gesture.
Called Joram in 2 Samuel 8:10.

chapters.n: David dedicates all these treasures to the Lord rather than keeping them. They become a fund for the future temple.
Abishai defeats 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt, probably south of the Dead Sea.

f.g: 2 Samuel 8:13 credits David as king; Psalm 60’s heading mentions Joab. Victories were credited to king and commanders alike.

chapters.n: Edom too comes under David’s rule. The refrain repeats: the Lord gave David victory wherever he went.

f.w: all the Edomites became David's servants

chapters.n: David reigns over all Israel with justice and righteousness—the ideal of a godly king, foreshadowing the Messiah’s righteous reign.
David’s chief officials are listed: Joab commands the army, and Jehoshaphat keeps the royal records.

f.g: Royal herald or secretary of state, who kept records and announced decrees.

chapters.n: Zadok and Abimelech serve as priests; Shavsha is the royal scribe.

f.g: Called Ahimelech in 2 Samuel 8:17; Abiathar also served as priest.
Also called Seraiah or Shisha; perhaps a foreign name.

chapters.n: Benaiah commands David’s foreign bodyguard, and David’s sons serve as chief officials. Where 2 Samuel calls David’s sons “priests,” Chronicles uses a term reserving priesthood for Levites.

f.g: Probably Cretans and Philistines—loyal mercenaries in David’s royal guard.

chapters.n: Nahash, king of Ammon (east of the Jordan), dies, and his son Hanun becomes king.

f.w: Nahash the king of the children of Ammon

chapters.n: David sends envoys to comfort Hanun, repaying an earlier kindness Nahash had shown him—perhaps during David’s years as a fugitive from Saul.

f.g: Hebrew hesed—loyal, covenant kindness.

f.w: his father shewed kindness to me

chapters.n: Hanun’s advisers convince him that David’s envoys are spies preparing for an invasion. Suspicion turns kindness into insult.

f.g: To scout for military weaknesses.

chapters.n: Hanun humiliates the envoys by shaving them and cutting their robes to expose them. In that culture, this was a deep public insult to David himself.

f.g: 2 Samuel 10:4 specifies half their beards—a grave dishonor for men of that culture.
Right up to their hips, leaving them exposed.

chapters.n: David kindly tells the shamed men to stay in Jericho until their beards grow back, sparing them further embarrassment.

f.g: Wait at Jericho, the first town west of the Jordan on their way home.

chapters.n: Realizing they have made David their enemy, the Ammonites pay a fortune to hire chariots and soldiers from Aramean kingdoms to the north.

f.g: Hateful; offensive (literally “a stench”).
An enormous sum—roughly 34 tons of silver.

chapters.n: The hired forces camp at Medeba, and the Ammonites gather for battle.

f.g: Possibly “chariots and charioteers”; 2 Samuel 10:6 gives the number as foot soldiers.
A town on the plateau east of the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: David sends Joab with the whole army of seasoned warriors.

f.w: the host of the mighty men
f.g: The army, including David’s elite warriors.

chapters.n: The Ammonites line up at their city gate while the Aramean mercenaries take the open field—trapping Israel between two armies.

f.g: Arranged their troops in battle formation.

chapters.n: Surrounded front and back, Joab takes the best troops himself to face the Arameans.

f.g: The best, most select soldiers.

chapters.n: He puts his brother Abishai in charge of the rest to face the Ammonites.
The brothers agree to help whichever one is in trouble—a simple picture of teamwork and mutual support.
Joab’s stirring words: be strong and brave for our people and God’s cities, and let the Lord do what seems good to Him. They will do their best and trust God with the outcome.

f.w: let the LORD do that which is good in his sight

chapters.n: Joab advances, and the Arameans flee.

f.g: Drew near; advanced.

chapters.n: Seeing their allies run, the Ammonites retreat into their city. Joab returns to Jerusalem.

f.g: Rabbah, the Ammonite capital (modern Amman, Jordan).

chapters.n: The defeated Arameans call for reinforcements from beyond the Euphrates under Shophach, Hadarezer’s commander.

f.g: East of the Euphrates.
Called Shobach in 2 Samuel 10:16.

chapters.n: David himself leads all Israel across the Jordan to meet them.
The Arameans are routed, and their commander is killed.

f.w: seven thousand men which fought in chariots
f.g: 2 Samuel 10:18 gives 700 chariots and 40,000 horsemen—differences likely from copying.

chapters.n: Hadarezer’s vassals make peace with David and become subject to him. The Arameans refuse to help Ammon again—Hanun’s insult has cost him his allies.

In spring, Joab besieges Rabbah, Ammon’s capital, while David stays in Jerusalem. 2 Samuel tells us this is when David sinned with Bathsheba; the chronicler leaves that story out, focusing on David’s role in God’s plan rather than repeating his failures.

f.w: at the time that kings go out to battle
f.g: Spring, after the rainy season, when armies could travel.
Ravaged; laid waste.

chapters.n: David takes the crown from the Ammonite king—or from their god Milcom—weighing about seventy-five pounds and set with a precious stone, and much plunder.

f.g: Hebrew malkam; can also be read as “Milcom,” the Ammonite god, whose idol may have worn the crown.
About 75 pounds (34 kg)—likely worn only briefly or ceremonially.

chapters.n: David puts the Ammonite people to work with saws, iron picks and axes—hard labor for the conquered. Older translations read it as torture, but many scholars favor forced labor.

f.g: The Hebrew can mean “set them to work at saws”; compare 2 Samuel 12:31.
Heavy tools with iron teeth for breaking up ground.

chapters.n: War breaks out again with the Philistines, and Sibbechai kills a descendant of the giants. The Philistines are subdued.

f.g: Descendants of the Rapha, a race of very tall warriors.

chapters.n: Elhanan kills Lahmi, brother of Goliath, whose spear was as thick as a weaver’s beam. This clarifies 2 Samuel 21:19, which, as copied, seems to say Elhanan killed Goliath himself.

f.g: The thick wooden rod on a loom—a very heavy spear shaft.

chapters.n: At Gath, a huge man with six fingers and six toes on each hand and foot is another descendant of the giants.

f.g: Twenty-four digits in all.

chapters.n: When he taunts Israel, as Goliath once had, David’s nephew Jonathan kills him.
These giants of Gath fell to David and his men. What once terrified Israel in the days of Moses and Saul is overcome by faith in God.

f.w: they fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants

chapters.n: Satan incites David to count Israel’s fighting men. The parallel in 2 Samuel says the Lord “moved” David; the chronicler makes clear that the tempter was Satan, while God permitted the test.

f.g: Hebrew “adversary” or “accuser.” This is one of the few Old Testament passages to use it as a proper name.
Take a military census—probably reflecting pride in his own strength rather than trust in God.

chapters.n: David orders Joab and the leaders to count everyone from Beer-sheba in the south to Dan in the north, so that he can know his total strength.

f.g: From one end of the land to the other.
The motive seems to be pride—David wanted to measure his power.

chapters.n: Joab objects: may God multiply the people a hundredfold, but why do this? Why bring guilt on Israel? Even the hard-nosed general senses that this is wrong.

f.g: A reason for guilt to fall on the nation.

f.w: an hundred times so many more

chapters.n: David overrules Joab, who reluctantly carries out the census throughout Israel.

f.w: the king's word prevailed against Joab

chapters.n: Joab reports 1,100,000 fighting men in Israel and 470,000 in Judah. The numbers differ from 2 Samuel, perhaps because of different counting methods or copying.

f.w: a thousand thousand and an hundred thousand
f.g: 1,100,000; 2 Samuel 24:9 gives 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah.
Able to fight.

chapters.n: Joab is so disgusted by the order that he leaves out Levi and Benjamin. Levi was exempt from military service by law, and Benjamin’s territory included the tabernacle at Gibeon.

f.g: Detestable; repugnant.

f.w: Levi and Benjamin counted he not

chapters.n: God is displeased and strikes Israel. A leader’s pride can bring consequences on many people.

f.w: God was displeased with this thing

chapters.n: David’s conscience awakens. He confesses honestly, asks God to take away his guilt, and admits he acted foolishly. Quick, sincere repentance marks David at his best.

f.g: Remove the guilt; forgive the sin.

chapters.n: The Lord speaks to Gad, David’s prophet.

f.g: A prophet who “sees” by revelation.

chapters.n: Gad brings David a choice of three consequences.

f.g: God lets David choose the form of the consequence.

chapters.n: Gad delivers the Lord’s message.

f.g: Choose for yourself.

chapters.n: The options: three years of famine, three months of military defeat, or three days of plague from the Lord’s angel.

f.g: 2 Samuel 24:13 reads seven years; the three-three-three pattern here may be original.
Plague; deadly epidemic disease.
Think it over and decide.

chapters.n: David chooses to fall into the Lord’s hands rather than man’s, because God’s mercies are great. Even in judgment, he trusts God’s character.

f.w: I am in a great strait
f.g: I am in great distress; a terrible dilemma.

f.w: for very great are his mercies

chapters.n: The plague strikes, and seventy thousand Israelites die.
As the angel prepares to destroy Jerusalem, the Lord relents and says, “Enough!” The angel stops beside the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. God’s mercy limits His judgments.

f.w: he repented him of the evil
f.g: He relented from the disaster—a human way of describing God’s mercy, not a change of character.
Called Araunah in 2 Samuel 24:16.

chapters.n: David sees the angel between heaven and earth with a drawn sword over Jerusalem. He and the elders, wearing sackcloth, fall face down in humility.

f.g: Rough goat-hair cloth worn as a sign of mourning and repentance.

chapters.n: David takes full responsibility: I sinned, not these sheep. Let the punishment fall on me and my family, not on the people. Like a true shepherd, he offers himself for his flock—a faint foreshadowing of Christ.

f.w: these sheep, what have they done?
be on me, and on my father's house
f.g: David asks that the punishment fall on himself and his own family instead of the nation.

chapters.n: Through Gad, the angel instructs David to build an altar at Ornan’s threshing floor. The place of judgment becomes the place of worship.

f.w: set up an altar unto the LORD

chapters.n: David obeys immediately, following the prophet’s word.

f.g: In obedience to the prophet’s message.

chapters.n: Ornan, threshing wheat, sees the angel; his four sons hide in fear.

f.g: Separating grain from stalks, done on high, open ground to catch the wind.

chapters.n: When the king arrives, Ornan bows to the ground before him.

f.w: bowed himself to David with his face to the ground
f.g: A sign of deep respect to a king.

chapters.n: David asks to buy the threshing floor at full price so he can build an altar and stop the plague.
Ornan generously offers it all for free—land, oxen for sacrifice, threshing sledges for firewood, and wheat for the grain offering.

f.g: The grain offering; “meat” in the KJV means food in general.
Wooden sledges dragged over grain to thresh it.

chapters.n: David refuses: “I will not… offer burnt offerings without cost.” True sacrifice to God must cost us something.

f.w: nor offer burnt offerings without cost

chapters.n: David pays 600 shekels of gold for the site. 2 Samuel records fifty shekels of silver—perhaps for the threshing floor alone, while Chronicles gives the price of the whole hilltop.

f.g: About 15 pounds (7 kg) of gold.

chapters.n: David builds the altar and offers sacrifices, and God answers with fire from heaven—the same sign that approved the tabernacle and later the temple.

f.w: he answered him from heaven by fire

chapters.n: The Lord commands the angel to sheathe his sword. Through repentance and sacrifice, the judgment ends.

f.w: he put up his sword again into the sheath
f.g: The judgment is finished.

chapters.n: Seeing that God accepted his offering there, David continues to sacrifice at this site.

f.g: God’s acceptance marked this as a holy place.

chapters.n: The old tabernacle and its altar were still at Gibeon, the official place of sacrifice at the time.
But David was afraid to travel to Gibeon because of the angel’s sword. This explains why Ornan’s threshing floor—Mount Moriah, where Abraham once offered Isaac—became the site of Solomon’s temple.

f.w: the sword of the angel of the LORD

chapters.n: After God answers by fire, David declares that this threshing floor will be the site of the Lord’s house and Israel’s altar. The place of mercy becomes the place of the temple.

f.w: This is the house of the LORD God

chapters.n: David begins preparing, assigning resident foreigners to cut building stones for the temple.

f.g: Non-Israelite residents living in the land.
Cut and dressed stones ready for building.

chapters.n: He stockpiles iron for nails and fittings and more bronze than could be weighed.

f.g: Clamps or fittings to join beams together.
Too much to weigh.

chapters.n: Phoenicians from Sidon and Tyre bring great quantities of cedar.

f.g: People of Sidon, a Phoenician city famed for timber and craftsmanship.

chapters.n: David reasons that Solomon is young and inexperienced, yet the temple must be magnificent and famous worldwide. So he prepares generously before his death—investing in a work he will never see completed.

f.g: Young and inexperienced.
Exceedingly magnificent.

chapters.n: David calls Solomon and formally charges him to build the Lord’s house.

f.g: Gave him a solemn commission.

chapters.n: David shares his heart with his son: he himself had wanted to build a house for the Lord’s name.
But God told David he could not build it because he had shed much blood in war. The temple, a house of peace, was to be built by a man of peace.
God promised a son who would be “a man of rest,” named Solomon, a name related to shalom, “peace.” Israel would have peace in his days.

f.g: Related to Hebrew shalom, “peace.”

chapters.n: Solomon will build God’s house, and God will be his Father and establish his throne forever—repeating the covenant of chapter 17.

f.w: he shall be my son, and I will be his father

chapters.n: David blesses Solomon: may the Lord be with you, and may you succeed in building His house.
David prays that God will give Solomon wisdom and understanding to keep His law. God later granted Solomon’s own request for wisdom.

f.w: the LORD give thee wisdom and understanding

chapters.n: Success depends on obedience to God’s law. David repeats the words God gave Joshua: be strong and courageous; don’t be afraid or discouraged.

f.w: be strong, and of good courage; dread not, nor be dismayed

chapters.n: David lists the vast treasures he gathered “in my trouble”—through hardship and wars. The enormous numbers emphasize lavish dedication to God.

f.g: Through great effort and hardship; or “in my affliction.”

f.w: an hundred thousand talents of gold
f.g: An immense sum, perhaps 3,750 tons; such figures likely stress abundance rather than exact accounting.

chapters.n: Skilled workers of every kind are ready—stonecutters, masons, carpenters and craftsmen.

f.g: Skilled craftsmen; “cunning” meant skillful.

chapters.n: With materials beyond counting, David urges Solomon: “Arise therefore, and be doing.” Preparation must lead to action.
David also commands Israel’s leaders to support Solomon. Building God’s house is a shared work.

f.g: Tribal leaders and officials.

chapters.n: David reminds them that God has given them peace and victory. Rest from enemies is the right time to build God’s house.

f.w: hath he not given you rest on every side?

chapters.n: The key charge: set your heart and soul to seek the Lord, then build His sanctuary so the ark can have a permanent home. Seeking God comes before building for Him.

f.w: set your heart and your soul to seek the LORD your God

f.g: The sacred utensils of the tabernacle.

chapters.n: In his old age David makes Solomon king. The chronicler summarizes briefly; 1 Kings 1 tells the dramatic story of rival claims to the throne.

f.g: Elderly, having lived a full life.

f.w: he made Solomon his son king

chapters.n: David gathers the leaders, priests and Levites to organize temple service. Chapters 23–27 describe this careful organization.
The Levites thirty years and older are counted: 38,000 men.

f.w: from the age of thirty years and upward

f.g: By head; one by one.

chapters.n: Their assignments: 24,000 oversee temple work, and 6,000 serve as officials and judges throughout the land.

f.g: To supervise or carry on the work.

chapters.n: Four thousand are gatekeepers and four thousand musicians, using instruments David himself made for praise.
David divides the Levites into rotating groups according to the three main families.

f.g: Divisions that took turns serving, like shifts.

chapters.n: The Gershonite branches begin with Laadan and Shimei.

f.g: Also called Libni (1 Chronicles 6:17).

chapters.n: Laadan’s three sons head family divisions.
Three more clan heads, also counted under Laadan’s family.

f.g: Probably a descendant of Laadan named after the clan ancestor.

chapters.n: Shimei’s four sons head more divisions.

f.g: Called Zizah in verse 11.

chapters.n: Two of Shimei’s sons had few children, so their families were counted as a single unit for service. The system adapts to real family circumstances.

f.g: Counted together as one family unit.

chapters.n: Kohath’s four sons founded the Kohathite branches.
Aaron and his descendants were set apart forever to handle the most holy things, burn incense, serve the Lord and bless the people in His name.
Moses, though the great lawgiver, did not pass priestly privilege to his sons; they were counted as ordinary Levites. Greatness did not create a dynasty.
Moses’ two sons are named.
Shebuel led Gershom’s descendants and later oversaw the temple treasuries.
Eliezer had only one son, Rehabiah, but Rehabiah’s descendants became very numerous. A small beginning can grow into a large family.

f.w: the sons of Rehabiah were very many

chapters.n: Shelomith led the descendants of Izhar.
The four leaders of Hebron’s branch.
The two leaders of Uzziel’s branch.
The Merarite families through Mahli and Mushi.
Eleazar had only daughters, who married their cousins, the sons of Kish, keeping the family’s inheritance within the clan as the law allowed.

f.g: Married them.

chapters.n: Mushi’s three sons head more Merarite divisions.

f.g: A Merarite clan head; the name appears in several Levite lists.

chapters.n: These were the Levite clan heads, now counted from age twenty, for temple service.

f.w: from the age of twenty years and upward
f.g: Numbers used ages thirty (4:3) and twenty-five (8:24); David lowers it to twenty for the larger temple workload.

chapters.n: David explains why: God has given Israel rest, and He will dwell in Jerusalem permanently.

f.w: that they may dwell in Jerusalem for ever
f.g: Or “He (God) dwells in Jerusalem forever.”

chapters.n: The Levites will no longer need to carry the tabernacle from place to place, so their duties shift to service in a permanent temple.

f.w: they shall no more carry the tabernacle

chapters.n: By David’s final instructions, Levites are enrolled from age twenty.

f.g: David’s final arrangements before his death.

chapters.n: The Levites assist the priests in the temple courts and rooms and help purify all the holy things.

f.w: to wait on the sons of Aaron

f.g: Ceremonial cleaning of sacred objects.

chapters.n: They prepare the showbread, grain offerings and baked goods, and keep all the weights and measures accurate.

f.g: Standards of quantity and length—ensuring honesty and accuracy.

chapters.n: Every morning and evening they stand to thank and praise the Lord. Daily devotion frames the day in worship.

f.w: every morning to thank and praise the LORD

f.g: In the evening.

chapters.n: They assist with burnt offerings on Sabbaths, new moons and appointed feasts.

f.g: Monthly festivals at the start of each lunar month.
Appointed festivals such as Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles.

chapters.n: In all, the Levites guard the sanctuary and support their priestly brothers. Every role, even behind the scenes, serves the Lord.

f.g: Carry out the duty; be responsible for.

chapters.n: Now the priests—Aaron’s descendants—are organized into divisions. The chapter starts with Aaron’s four sons.
Nadab and Abihu died without children after offering unauthorized fire, so the priesthood passed through Eleazar and Ithamar.

f.w: Nadab and Abihu died before their father

chapters.n: David works with Zadok (from Eleazar’s line) and Ahimelech (from Ithamar’s line) to organize the priests.

f.w: Zadok of the sons of Eleazar
Ahimelech of the sons of Ithamar

chapters.n: Eleazar’s line had more family heads, so it received sixteen divisions and Ithamar’s eight—twenty-four in all.

f.g: Sixteen family heads, each leading a priestly division.

chapters.n: The divisions were assigned by lot so that both families shared equally in honor, since both had produced leaders of the sanctuary. Lots left the choice to God and prevented favoritism.

f.g: Impartially, the two families alternating.

chapters.n: A Levite scribe, Shemaiah, officially recorded the drawing before the king and leaders, alternating between Eleazar’s and Ithamar’s families. Careful records ensured fairness and order.

f.g: Recorded the results in front of witnesses.

chapters.n: The first lot fell to Jehoiarib and the second to Jedaiah. Each division served in the temple for a week at a time, in rotation.
The third and fourth divisions.
The fifth and sixth divisions.
The eighth division belonged to Abijah. Centuries later, the priest Zacharias, father of John the Baptist, served in this course when the angel Gabriel appeared to him.
The ninth and tenth divisions; Jeshua was a common priestly name after the exile.

f.g: A form of Joshua—the same name as Jesus.

chapters.n: The eleventh and twelfth divisions.

f.g: “God restores.”

chapters.n: The thirteenth and fourteenth divisions.

f.g: A priestly division mentioned only here.

chapters.n: The fifteenth and sixteenth divisions, including Immer’s, whose descendant Pashur struck Jeremiah.
The seventeenth and eighteenth divisions.

f.g: A family name later carved on a priestly tomb in Jerusalem’s Kidron Valley.

chapters.n: The nineteenth and twentieth divisions.

f.g: The same name as Ezekiel, “God strengthens.”

chapters.n: The twenty-first and twenty-second divisions.

f.g: Also the name of one of the temple’s two bronze pillars (1 Kings 7:21).

chapters.n: The twenty-third and twenty-fourth divisions complete the list. This system of twenty-four courses was still in use in New Testament times.
Each division came to the temple in its turn according to the pattern God gave Aaron. Order in worship reflects the God of order.

f.w: as the LORD God of Israel had commanded him

f.g: Assigned order or schedule.

chapters.n: The chronicler now lists the remaining Levite family heads, updating the list from chapter 23 by a generation.

f.g: Same as Shebuel (1 Chronicles 23:16).

chapters.n: Rehabiah’s branch, descended from Moses, was led by Isshiah.
The Izharites, led by Shelomoth and his son Jahath.

f.g: Same as Shelomith (1 Chronicles 23:18).

chapters.n: Hebron’s four leaders are repeated from the earlier list.
Uzziel’s branch through Michah and his son Shamir.
Michah’s brother Isshiah and his son Zechariah.

f.g: Called Jesiah in 1 Chronicles 23:20.

chapters.n: The Merarites, including a branch through Jaaziah not listed earlier.

f.g: A Merarite branch otherwise unknown.

chapters.n: Jaaziah’s descendants are named.

f.g: May mean “his son” rather than a name.

chapters.n: Mahli’s son Eleazar had no sons.
Kish’s son Jerahmeel headed his own division.

f.g: A Levite; not the Judahite Jerahmeel of chapter 2.

chapters.n: Mushi’s sons close the list of Levite family heads.

f.g: Called Jeremoth in 1 Chronicles 23:23.

chapters.n: The Levites also cast lots for their duties, just like the priests, with senior and junior families treated alike. In God’s service, rank did not decide one’s place.

f.w: the principal fathers over against their younger brethren
f.g: The heads of the senior families were treated the same as the junior ones.

chapters.n: David and the leaders set apart the families of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun to “prophesy” with instruments. Inspired music was seen as a form of prophecy—declaring God’s truth and praise.

f.g: To proclaim God’s word and praise through inspired song.
Set apart for a special assignment.

chapters.n: Asaph’s four sons served under their father’s direction, following the king’s arrangements.

f.g: Under Asaph’s direction and supervision.

f.w: according to the order of the king

chapters.n: Jeduthun’s six sons served under him, prophesying with the lyre in thanks and praise.

f.w: to give thanks and to praise the LORD

chapters.n: Heman’s fourteen sons are named. Read together, the last nine names in Hebrew sound like a short prayer-poem: “Be gracious to me, LORD… you are my God… I have magnified and exalted [your] help… I have spoken visions.”

f.g: “I have magnified.”
“I have exalted (your) help.”
“Visions.”

chapters.n: Heman was the king’s seer, and God blessed him with fourteen sons and three daughters—a sign of divine favor. His family “lifted up the horn,” exalting God or Heman’s honor.

f.g: A prophet serving the king.
An idiom for increasing strength or honor; here perhaps of praising God.

chapters.n: All of them made music in the Lord’s house under their fathers, using cymbals, harps and lyres, according to the king’s directions. Families served together.

f.w: under the hands of their father
f.g: Taught and directed by their fathers—music passed down through families.

chapters.n: There were 288 trained musicians in all—twenty-four groups of twelve.

f.g: Skilled.

chapters.n: They cast lots for their turns of duty, young and old, teacher and student alike. In God’s service, all stand on equal footing.

f.g: Duty group alongside duty group.
The master the same as the student.

chapters.n: The first lot fell to Joseph of Asaph’s family and the second to Gedaliah of Jeduthun’s. Each course had twelve musicians.

f.g: A son of Asaph (verse 2).
“The LORD is great”; a son of Jeduthun.

chapters.n: The third lot went to Zaccur, Asaph’s eldest listed son.

f.g: “Remembered”; a son of Asaph.

chapters.n: The fourth lot went to Izri of Jeduthun’s family.

f.g: Called Zeri in verse 3.

chapters.n: The fifth lot went to Nethaniah, a son of Asaph.

f.g: “Gift of the LORD.”

chapters.n: The sixth lot was the first to fall to Heman’s family, through Bukkiah.

f.g: Heman’s firstborn listed son (verse 4).

chapters.n: The seventh lot went to Jesharelah, Asaph’s fourth son—completing Asaph’s four courses.

f.g: Called Asarelah in verse 2.

chapters.n: The eighth lot went to Jeshaiah of Jeduthun’s family.

f.g: A form of the name Isaiah, “the LORD saves.”

chapters.n: The ninth lot went to Mattaniah, a son of Heman. By this point all three music families are well represented.

f.g: “Gift of the LORD.”

chapters.n: The tenth lot went to Shimei, a son of Jeduthun not named in verse 3—making Jeduthun’s six sons complete.

f.g: Jeduthun’s sixth son, missing from verse 3’s list of names.

chapters.n: The eleventh lot went to Azareel of Heman’s family.

f.g: Called Uzziel in verse 4.

chapters.n: The twelfth lot went to Hashabiah of Jeduthun’s family—the halfway point of the twenty-four courses.

f.g: “The LORD has taken account.”

chapters.n: The thirteenth lot went to Shubael, a son of Heman.

f.g: Called Shebuel in verse 4.

chapters.n: The fourteenth lot went to Mattithiah, the last of Jeduthun’s sons to be assigned.

f.g: “Gift of the LORD”; also a Levite musician in 1 Chronicles 15:18, 21.

chapters.n: From the fifteenth lot onward, every course falls to Heman’s large family, beginning with Jeremoth.

f.g: Called Jerimoth in verse 4.

chapters.n: The sixteenth lot went to Hananiah, whose name means “the LORD is gracious”—the first words of the name-prayer in verse 4.

f.g: “Be gracious, O LORD” or “the LORD is gracious.”

chapters.n: The seventeenth lot went to Joshbekashah, whose name may mean “sitting in hardship.”

f.g: Possibly “dwelling in difficulty”—part of the poetic sequence of names.

chapters.n: The eighteenth lot went to Hanani, “be gracious to me.”

f.g: “Be gracious to me”; a name also borne by a later prophet (2 Chronicles 16:7).

chapters.n: The nineteenth lot went to Mallothi, “I have spoken.”

f.g: Possibly “I have uttered” or “I have spoken.”

chapters.n: The twentieth lot went to Eliathah, “you are my God.”

f.g: “You are my God.”

chapters.n: The twenty-first lot went to Hothir, “he has given abundantly.”

f.g: Possibly “He has caused to abound.”

chapters.n: The twenty-second lot went to Giddalti, “I have magnified.”
The twenty-third lot went to Mahazioth, “visions”—recalling that this music was considered a kind of prophecy.

f.g: “Visions.”

chapters.n: The last lot went to Romamti-ezer, “I have exalted help.” The twenty-four courses of singers now match the twenty-four courses of priests, a complete order of worship.

f.g: “I have lifted up (God’s) help.”

chapters.n: The gatekeepers are organized next. They guarded the temple entrances, protected its treasures and kept order. Meshelemiah came from the Korahite family.

f.g: Gatekeepers, not baggage carriers.
Probably Ebiasaph, a Korahite ancestor (1 Chronicles 9:19), not Asaph the musician.

chapters.n: Meshelemiah’s sons are listed in birth order, beginning with Zechariah, who guarded the tent of meeting.
Meshelemiah’s fifth through seventh sons complete his family.

f.g: The full form of the name John, “the LORD is gracious.”

chapters.n: Obed-edom—whose house sheltered the ark for three months—had many sons who became gatekeepers.
Obed-edom had eight sons “for God blessed him.” The blessing promised when the ark stayed in his house is seen in his large family.
Obed-edom’s grandsons through Shemaiah became leaders of their family because of their ability.

f.g: Capable, strong men—here suited to guard duty.

chapters.n: Shemaiah’s sons and relatives, all strong and capable.

f.g: “He is my God”; also the name of Job’s young friend (Job 32:2).

chapters.n: Obed-edom’s family supplied sixty-two capable gatekeepers—the largest group.

f.g: Sixty-two.
Strong, qualified men for the work.

chapters.n: Meshelemiah’s family supplied eighteen.

f.g: Together with the other families, about ninety-three senior gatekeepers are named.

chapters.n: Hosah, a Merarite, made his son Simri chief even though he was not the firstborn—perhaps because of his ability or because the firstborn had died.

f.w: though he was not the firstborn

chapters.n: Hosah’s other sons are listed; his family numbered thirteen.

f.g: A Levite gatekeeper, not the later high priest.

chapters.n: These leaders formed the gatekeeper divisions, serving in shifts just like their fellow Levites.

f.g: Taking turns in duty shifts, matched to their brethren.

chapters.n: They cast lots for each gate, small families and large alike, ensuring fairness.

f.w: as well the small as the great

chapters.n: The east gate—the main entrance—went to Shelemiah (Meshelemiah). The north went to his son Zechariah, praised as a wise counselor.

f.g: Same as Meshelemiah (verse 1).
A man of good judgment; gatekeepers needed wisdom as well as strength.

chapters.n: The south gate went to Obed-edom, and his sons guarded the storehouse.

f.g: “Storehouses”—buildings for temple supplies.

chapters.n: The west gate, called Shallecheth, on the road going up, went to Shuppim and Hosah.

f.g: A gate name meaning possibly “casting out,” perhaps where refuse was taken out.

f.w: the causeway of the going up
f.g: An ascending road or ramp leading to the temple.

chapters.n: The daily guard: six at the east, four at the north and south, and two pairs at the storehouse.

f.g: The east gate, facing the main approach, received the largest guard.

chapters.n: On the west side, four guarded the road and two guarded the Parbar, making twenty-four posts in all.

f.g: A colonnade or court on the temple’s west side; the exact meaning is uncertain.

chapters.n: These were the gatekeeper divisions from the families of Korah and Merari.

f.g: Korahites, descendants of Korah through Kore.

chapters.n: Other Levites were placed over the temple treasuries and the dedicated gifts.

f.w: the treasures of the dedicated things
f.g: Gifts consecrated to God, such as war plunder set apart for the temple.

chapters.n: Gershonite Levites of Laadan’s family, led by Jehieli, oversaw treasuries.

f.g: Probably the same as Jehiel (1 Chronicles 23:8).

chapters.n: Jehieli’s sons Zetham and Joel were in charge of the temple treasury.
Next come the Kohathite families: the Amramites, Izharites, Hebronites and Uzzielites.

f.g: Descendants of Amram, father of Moses and Aaron.

chapters.n: Shebuel, a descendant of Moses, was chief officer over the treasuries.

f.w: Shebuel the son of Gershom, the son of Moses
f.g: “Son” here means descendant; many generations lie between.

chapters.n: Through Moses’ other son Eliezer came a line leading to Shelomith.
Shelomith and his relatives managed all the treasures dedicated by David and his military leaders.

f.g: Army officers commanding large and small units.

chapters.n: These treasures came from plunder won in battle and were dedicated to maintain the Lord’s house. Victories God gave were returned to God.

f.w: Out of the spoils won in battles

chapters.n: Gifts dedicated by Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab were also under Shelomith’s care. Generations of leaders had contributed to God’s house.
Chenaniah and his sons from the Izharites handled duties outside the temple, serving as officials and judges across Israel.

f.g: Work outside the temple—civil administration and judging.

chapters.n: Hashabiah and 1,700 Hebronites served west of the Jordan in both religious and royal affairs. Spiritual and civic service went hand in hand.

f.w: in all the business of the LORD, and in the service of the king

chapters.n: In David’s fortieth and final year, a search of records found capable Hebronite men at Jazer in Gilead, east of the Jordan.

f.w: the fortieth year of the reign of David
f.g: David’s last year, about 970 BC.

chapters.n: David appointed 2,700 of them as leaders over the tribes east of the Jordan for all matters of God and of the king—ensuring the distant tribes were not neglected.

f.w: every matter pertaining to God, and affairs of the king

chapters.n: Having organized the temple, the chronicler turns to the kingdom’s civil and military structure. The army served in twelve monthly rotations of 24,000 men—a citizen militia rather than a huge standing army.

f.w: came in and went out month by month
f.g: Each division served one month a year, then returned home.
Rotating divisions.

chapters.n: Jashobeam, chief of David’s mighty men, commanded the first month’s division.
Jashobeam was from Judah’s Perez clan—David’s own family line—and was chief of all the commanders for the first month.
Dodai the Ahohite led the second month, with Mikloth as his officer.

f.g: Dodo, father of Eleazar, one of the three mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:12).

chapters.n: Benaiah, son of Jehoiada the priest, led the third month’s division.

f.g: Describes Jehoiada, Benaiah’s father, a leading priest.

chapters.n: This Benaiah was famous among the Thirty; his son Ammizabad served under him.
Asahel, Joab’s brother, headed the fourth month, followed by his son Zebadiah. Since Asahel died early in David’s reign, this may reflect an early arrangement or a post named in his honor.
Shamhuth led the fifth month’s division.

f.g: Probably Shammoth the Harorite (1 Chronicles 11:27); Izrahite may mean a descendant of Zerah.

chapters.n: Ira of Tekoa led the sixth month.

f.w: Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite

chapters.n: Helez of Ephraim led the seventh month.
Sibbecai, who killed a giant, led the eighth month.

f.g: Descendants of Zerah, a clan of Judah.

chapters.n: Abiezer from Anathoth in Benjamin led the ninth month.
Maharai of Netophah led the tenth month.
Benaiah of Pirathon in Ephraim—a different Benaiah—led the eleventh month.
Heldai of Netophah, descended from Othniel the judge, led the twelfth month. All twelve commanders came from David’s mighty men.

f.g: Called Heled in 1 Chronicles 11:30.

chapters.n: Next come the leaders of the tribes, starting with Reuben and Simeon.

f.g: The tribal chief representing Reuben.

chapters.n: Levi had its own leader, and Aaron’s priestly line was led by Zadok.
Judah’s leader was Elihu, one of David’s brothers—probably Eliab, his eldest.

f.w: Elihu, one of the brethren of David
f.g: Possibly Eliab (1 Samuel 16:6), or simply a kinsman.

chapters.n: Leaders of Zebulun and Naphtali.

f.g: Naphtali’s chief, otherwise unknown.

chapters.n: Ephraim’s leader shared the original name of Joshua—Hoshea; Manasseh west of the Jordan had its own chief.

f.g: “Salvation”; Joshua’s original name (Numbers 13:16).

chapters.n: Leaders of eastern Manasseh in Gilead and of Benjamin. Benjamin’s chief was a son of Abner, Saul’s general—a sign of reconciliation with Saul’s house.
Dan’s leader completes the list. Gad and Asher are not mentioned, perhaps to keep the number at twelve with Levi and Aaron counted separately.

f.w: These were the princes of the tribes of Israel
f.g: Twelve leaders, though the tribal list differs from others.

chapters.n: David did not count those under twenty, remembering God’s promise to multiply Israel like the stars. Counting everyone would have implied doubt in that promise.

f.w: like to the stars of the heavens

chapters.n: Joab’s census was never finished because of God’s wrath, and the results were not entered in David’s official records.

f.w: there fell wrath for it against Israel

chapters.n: The king’s property managers are listed, starting with officials over the royal treasuries and storehouses throughout the land.

f.g: Fortified towers or outposts.

chapters.n: Ezri supervised the farm workers on royal lands.

f.g: Plowing and cultivating fields.

chapters.n: Shimei oversaw the vineyards and Zabdi the wine supplies.

f.g: The produce of the vineyards.

chapters.n: Baal-hanan managed olive and sycamore-fig trees in the western foothills, and Joash the oil supplies.

f.g: Sycamore-figs, valued for fruit and timber; not the North American sycamore.
The Shephelah, the foothills between the coast and the hill country.

chapters.n: Shitrai oversaw cattle grazing in the fertile Sharon plain, and Shaphat cattle in the valleys.

f.g: The coastal plain north of Joppa, rich pastureland.

chapters.n: Fittingly, an Ishmaelite—from a people famous for camel herding—managed the camels, and Jehdeiah the donkeys.

f.g: A foreigner trusted with royal property; his name may mean “camel driver.”

chapters.n: Jaziz, a Hagrite, oversaw the flocks. These officials managed King David’s considerable wealth.

f.g: A Hagrite, from a desert people (1 Chronicles 5:10).
Property or possessions.

chapters.n: David’s inner circle: his uncle Jonathan, a wise counselor and scribe, and Jehiel, who tutored or attended the king’s sons.

f.g: Possibly “relative”; Hebrew dod can mean uncle or kinsman.
Perhaps their tutor or guardian.

chapters.n: Ahithophel was the king’s counselor and Hushai the king’s friend. Ahithophel later betrayed David by joining Absalom, while Hushai stayed loyal and foiled his advice.

f.g: A title for a trusted royal friend and adviser.

chapters.n: After Ahithophel, Jehoiada and Abiathar served as counselors, and Joab commanded the army. David’s kingdom was carefully ordered, ready to pass to Solomon.

f.w: the general of the king's army was Joab

chapters.n: Near the end of his life, David gathers every level of leadership in Israel — tribal heads, army commanders, and the managers of royal property — to Jerusalem for a solemn public handoff of the temple project to Solomon.

f.g: In rotating shifts; 1 Chronicles 27 lists twelve divisions that each served the king one month a year.

chapters.n: An old king rising to his feet shows how much this moment matters to him. David calls the people his “brethren” and explains that he had longed to build a resting place for the ark, and had already gathered materials.

f.g: The ark was pictured as the footstool of the invisible divine King enthroned above the cherubim.

chapters.n: God had told David no. The temple was to be a house of peace, and David’s life had been spent in war. His disappointment becomes a lesson that God may assign a sacred work to someone else.

f.w: thou hast been a man of war

chapters.n: David traces God’s choosing step by step: the tribe of Judah, the family of Jesse, and finally David himself, the youngest son. His kingship was a gift, not an achievement.

f.w: he hath chosen Judah to be the ruler

f.g: He was pleased with me; he took delight in choosing me.

chapters.n: Among David’s many sons, God chose Solomon. Notice the phrase “the kingdom of the LORD” — the Chronicler stresses that the true King of Israel is God, and David’s heirs only sit on His throne.

f.w: the throne of the kingdom of the LORD

chapters.n: David quotes God’s promise that Solomon would build the temple and be treated as God’s own son. This father–son covenant language later points forward to the Messiah, the greater Son of David.
The promise of a lasting kingdom comes with a condition: Solomon must keep obeying, as he is doing now. God’s blessings in covenant are tied to faithfulness.

f.g: If he remains firm and steady.

chapters.n: Turning to the whole assembly, David charges them before both the people and God himself to keep every commandment, so they can keep the promised land and pass it to their children.

f.w: in the audience of our God
f.g: In God’s hearing — He is a witness to this charge.

chapters.n: One of the great verses of the Old Testament. David tells Solomon to truly know God and serve Him wholeheartedly and willingly, because God sees every thought. Seek Him and He will be found — forsake Him and lose Him.

f.g: Hebrew lev shalem — a whole, undivided heart; complete loyalty, not flawlessness.

f.w: if thou seek him, he will be found of thee

chapters.n: A short, punchy charge: God has chosen you for this — be strong and get it done. Divine calling is paired with personal effort.
David hands Solomon the detailed plan for the temple — its entry porch, buildings, storerooms, upper rooms, and the innermost room where the mercy seat would rest.

f.g: Hebrew tavnit — a model or blueprint, the same word used for the tabernacle plan shown to Moses.

f.w: the place of the mercy seat
f.g: The holy of holies, where the ark’s gold lid symbolized God’s throne of atonement.

chapters.n: Importantly, David received this plan “by the spirit.” Like the tabernacle before it, the temple was designed by revelation, not human imagination.

f.g: Or ‘that he had in his spirit/mind’; the Chronicler presents it as revealed.
Spoils and gifts set apart for God’s house.

chapters.n: The plan included not only buildings but organization: the rotating divisions of priests and Levites and all the tools for temple worship. Order in God’s house matters as much as architecture.
David even set aside exact weights of gold and silver for each tool. Nothing was left to chance — sacred things were prepared with care and precision.

f.g: Utensils or vessels used in the service.

chapters.n: Gold and silver were measured for each lampstand and its lamps. These lights recalled the tabernacle’s menorah, a symbol of God’s presence and light among His people.

f.g: Lampstands holding oil lamps, not wax candles.

chapters.n: Gold was given for the tables of shewbread, where loaves were set out before the Lord continually.

f.g: ‘Bread of the Presence’ — twelve loaves kept before God, renewed each Sabbath.

chapters.n: Even the smaller utensils — forks for handling meat, bowls, cups, and basins — had their own measured gold or silver. Every part of worship was treated as holy.

f.g: Large forks used to handle sacrificial meat.

chapters.n: Refined gold was set aside for the incense altar and for the golden cherubim whose wings overshadowed the ark — pictured here as God’s chariot-throne.

f.g: The cherubim were seen as the throne-chariot of God, as in Ezekiel’s vision.

chapters.n: David testifies that the Lord made the plan clear to him in writing, by His hand resting on David. The temple design came by revelation, much as Moses received the tabernacle pattern.

f.g: An idiom for the power of God’s Spirit coming upon a prophet.

chapters.n: David repeats the encouragement Moses once gave Joshua: be strong, don’t be afraid, God won’t abandon you until the work is done. It is a promise to anyone given a hard assignment from God.

f.w: he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee

chapters.n: Solomon would not work alone: priests, Levites, skilled and willing craftsmen, leaders, and people would all support him. God’s work is a shared effort of willing hearts.
David tells the assembly that Solomon is young and inexperienced, while the task is enormous — because this building is not a palace for a man but for the Lord God himself.

f.g: Hebrew birah — a fortress or citadel; here the temple as the great King’s dwelling.

chapters.n: David lists the materials he has stockpiled with all his strength: metals, wood, and every kind of precious and colored stone, plus marble in abundance.

f.g: Glittering or sparkling stones, perhaps inlaid or mosaic stones.
Various colors.

chapters.n: Beyond what he gathered as king, David now gives from his personal fortune because he loves God’s house. His gift is a model of personal sacrifice beyond duty.

f.g: My own private treasure, not the royal or national funds.

chapters.n: David’s personal gift is enormous: about 3,000 talents of fine gold from Ophir and 7,000 talents of silver, to cover the temple walls. A talent weighed roughly 75 pounds (34 kg).

f.g: A distant land famous for fine gold, perhaps in southern Arabia, East Africa, or India; its exact location is uncertain.
A large unit of weight, about 34 kg (75 lb).

chapters.n: After giving his own wealth, David turns to the people with a question: who else will willingly dedicate themselves to the Lord today? Giving begins with the leader’s example.

f.g: Literally ‘fill his hand’ — a phrase used for ordaining priests; here, to dedicate oneself freely.

chapters.n: The leaders respond at once, giving willingly. Family heads, tribal princes, army officers, and royal administrators all follow David’s lead.

The leaders’ gifts are vast: gold, silver, bronze, and iron by the thousands of talents. The “drams” are likely the Persian daric, a later coin the Chronicler used to help his readers grasp the value.

f.g: Hebrew ’adarkonim — probably darics, Persian gold coins, an updated measure for the Chronicler’s readers.

chapters.n: Those who owned precious stones gave them to the temple treasury, managed by Jehiel, a Levite from the clan of Gershon.
The joy came not from the size of the gifts but from the willing, wholehearted way they were given. Generous giving made both people and king glad.
David leads the congregation in a prayer of praise, blessing the God of Israel — that is, of Jacob, their ancestor — forever.

f.g: Jacob, renamed Israel, the father of the twelve tribes.

chapters.n: A majestic hymn: all greatness, power, glory, victory, and majesty belong to God, because everything in heaven and earth is His. Many Christians recognize this language in the closing words of the Lord’s Prayer.
David confesses that riches and honor come from God, who rules over all and alone can make anyone great or strong. Human success is a gift, not a reason for pride.

f.w: riches and honour come of thee

chapters.n: A simple turn to gratitude: “we thank thee, and praise thy glorious name.” Praise naturally follows recognizing God’s gifts.
Humbly David asks: who are we that we could give like this? Everything comes from God; we only give back what was already His. This is the heart of true stewardship.

f.w: of thine own have we given thee

chapters.n: Life is brief and we are only passing through. Like Abraham and the patriarchs, Israel lives as guests on God’s earth; our days fade like a shadow.
David repeats the point for emphasis: all this wealth gathered for God’s house came from God’s own hand and still belongs to Him.
God tests hearts and delights in honesty. David says he gave with an upright heart, and now rejoices to see his people giving just as freely.
David prays that God will keep this willing spirit alive in the people’s hearts forever and turn their hearts firmly toward Him. Good moments fade unless God sustains them.

f.g: The inner inclinations and purposes of the mind.

chapters.n: For his son, David asks one thing: a whole, loyal heart to keep God’s laws and finish the temple. A father’s greatest wish is for his child’s faithfulness.

f.g: God’s solemn declarations of His will — His covenant decrees.

chapters.n: David invites everyone to bless the Lord, and they bow low in worship before God and in respect before the king, His anointed.
The next day they offer three thousand animals in burnt offerings along with many other sacrifices — a great feast of worship for the whole nation.

f.g: Wine poured out alongside sacrifices.

chapters.n: The people feast joyfully in God’s presence and anoint Solomon king a “second time” — a public confirmation of his earlier hurried coronation. Zadok is anointed as priest.
Solomon sits on “the throne of the LORD” — another reminder that Israel’s king ruled on God’s behalf. He prospers, and all Israel obeys him.
Leaders, warriors, and even David’s other sons pledge loyalty to Solomon. The Chronicler skips the rivalries told in 1 Kings and emphasizes unity.

f.g: Literally ‘gave the hand under’ — a gesture of allegiance.

chapters.n: God greatly honored Solomon before the people, giving him a royal splendor no king of Israel had known before.
A summary of David’s life: the shepherd boy, Jesse’s son, became king over all Israel.
David reigned forty years — seven in Hebron over Judah, then thirty-three in Jerusalem over all Israel.

f.w: seven years reigned he in Hebron

chapters.n: David died old and satisfied with life, rich and honored, and Solomon took his place. “Full of days” describes a life completed, not cut short.

f.g: Satisfied with a long life, as was said of Abraham and Isaac.

chapters.n: The Chronicler names his sources: records kept by three prophets who knew David — Samuel, Nathan, and Gad. Much of this material appears in our books of Samuel and Kings.

f.g: A seer is a prophet who sees by God’s power.

chapters.n: These records cover David’s whole reign, his might, and the events that came upon him, Israel, and the surrounding kingdoms. With David’s death, the Chronicler turns to Solomon.

f.w: the times that went over him
f.g: The events and circumstances that passed over him.
